10539-in-the-riding-school-chats-with-es:
Theo. Stephenson Browne published this riding book in 1890, in chats with a pupil named Esmeralda. Browne dedicates it to his French, English, and American masters, and opens with a verse on riding side by side, laughing and chatting. The book teaches riding as a social art, not merely as sport.

Lessons treat dress, mounting, slippery reins, trotting without a horse, voltes, music rides, class distances, and military evolutions. Esmeralda's trials, a critical spectator, and fun in the dressing room add humor. Readers get a charming, period guide to horsemanship for ladies and gentlemen.
1124-troilus-and-cressida:
During the siege of Troy, Troilus loves Cressida, who is traded to the Greeks and soon takes a new lover. Meanwhile Greek and Trojan heroes squabble over honor, rank, and a war no one quite believes in. William Shakespeare's bitter play mixes a love plot with camp satire and ends without comfort.

Achilles sulks, Ajax struts, Ulysses schemes, and Thersites jeers at them all. The play's tone is dark and modern, closer to satire than to romance. Long neglected on stage, it now draws readers who like Shakespeare at his most skeptical about heroes and war.
12316-true-tilda:
A. T. Quiller-Couch wrote True Tilda as a children novel, published in 1909. The heroine, Tilda, is nine years old and belongs to show-folk, traveling performers whose code of loyalty shapes her conduct.

The story opens in a hospital ward, where Tilda, recovering herself, watches a gaunt woman brought in with acute pneumonia, feverish and delirious. Tilda sharp curiosity and kindness bind her to the stranger, and the tale follows the pair down river paths, past meadows, locks, and hanging copses. Quiller-Couch writes much of the dialogue in working-class slang and dialect of a century ago. The novel blends adventure with a moral of steadfast friendship.
13003-pioneers-in-canada:
Sir Harry Johnston's 1912 volume, part of his Pioneer Library, tells the story of white settlement in Canada for young readers. With colored plates by E. Wallcousins, it moves from early voyages to the growth of colonies along the St. Lawrence and the coasts. Johnston writes as a historian of empire, proud of explorers and settlers, and frank about the cost of their advance.

Chapters cover cod fishing off Newfoundland, Jamestown's shadow over the north, French and English rivalry, and the fate of Native peoples such as the Beothuk. Johnston condemns the hunting down of the Beothuk by fishermen and fur hunters in strong terms. The book thus mixes adventure with a hard record of how settlement displaced the peoples who lived there first.
13095-journal-of-a-voyage-across-the-atl:
George Moore, Esq., printed this journal for private circulation in London in 1845, after a voyage across the Atlantic and back in 1844. He wrote it for friends who kept asking about his American trip, and he says he left his first impressions unrevised. The journal runs day by day, from shipboard to Philadelphia, Canada, and home.

Moore praises a clean Philadelphia hotel, admires the Fairmount waterworks as both useful and ornamental, and notes men who rose from nothing to wealth. In Toronto he finds plank footpaths, a stalled college, and election bustle, and he dislikes a prison where men lie idle. The book's charm is its unpolished honesty, a traveler's notes kept in the moment, not dressed up after.
14301-atlantida:
Pierre Benoit's Atlantida, translated by Mary C. Tongue and Mary Ross, opens with a warning from Plato's Critias: do not be surprised to hear barbarians called by Grecian names. A letter dated Hassi-Inifel, November 1903, frames the tale: Lieutenant Ferrières entrusts a manuscript to Sergeant Chatelain for delivery to M. Leroux, to be disclosed only after delay. The Sahara, the Tuareg, and a lost queen await inside.

Morhange, the narrator's companion, chases Greek spirits in Tuareg mountains. Pomponius Mela, he notes, places Egipans, Blemyens, Gamphasantes, and satyrs there: naked wanderers, headless men with faces on chests, and beings human only in face. Antinea, he insists, will unlock remarkable discoveries. Paris interludes add comedy, as a narrator escorts Tuareg visitors, dines with them, and faces bills of forty thousand francs. Adventure, erudition, and desert mystery blend in a French classic of lost worlds.
1528-troilus-and-cressida:
Shakespeare's Trojan play sets the Greek camp against Troy's walls, where Troilus loves Cressida, Pandarus brokers their meeting, and the war grinds on around them. Achilles sulks in his tent, Hector debates honour, and Ulysses schemes, while Cressida, traded to the Greeks, proves faithless in the eyes of a bitter age.

The play refuses heroes: Greeks and Trojans alike are proud, lecherous, and tired of war. Its ending is bleak and unresolved. Troilus and Cressida is Shakespeare's most cynical work, a problem play that questions honour, love, and the very idea of heroic war.
18378-catholic-problems-in-western-canad:
George Thomas Daly, a Redemptorist priest, wrote this 1921 study of Catholic problems in western Canada, published at Toronto by Macmillan of Canada. Archbishop O. E. Mathieu of Regina wrote the preface, and the book is dedicated to the Catholic hierarchy of Canada. Daly writes as the West called for priests, schools, and missions, and the East answered.

Part one treats religious problems. It covers the call of the West and the Catholic Church Extension Society. It also treats the Ruthenian problem, a field secretary for missionary work, the church union movement, and the apostolate to non-Catholics. Readers get a church history from inside the work: a young Catholic West, its peoples, its missions, and the practical problems of building a church across great distances.
18876-woman-triumphant-la-maja-desnuda:
Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's novel, translated by Hayward Keniston and published by Dutton in 1920, takes its Spanish title, La Maja Desnuda, from a famous Goya painting. The author's note explains the maja: showy, gay women of Madrid's lower streets, famed for dancing and for showing themselves at bullfights and festivals.

When the novel first appeared in Spain, some readers claimed its leading pair were a real painter and a real lady, a charge the author firmly denies. He insists his characters are new types, drawn in fragments from life and remade by imagination, as a painter paints rather than photographs. The note frames a novel drawn from Madrid's art world, whose plot lies beyond the front matter.
18947-the-younger-edda-also-called-snorr:
Rasmus B. Anderson's English version of the Younger Edda, also called Snorri's Edda or the Prose Edda, presents the great medieval Icelandic handbook of Norse mythology, in an edition copyrighted in 1879. The volume translates the foreword, the Fooling of Gylfe, the afterwords, Brage's Talk, and key passages on poetical diction, with an introduction, notes, vocabulary, and index.

The tales explain how the gods formed man and woman from two trees, breathing life into Ask and Embla and giving them a garden in Midgard. They tell how the world began from the great abyss Ginungagap before heaven, earth, and sea were shaped. Anderson was a former professor of Scandinavian languages and minister to Denmark. He offers English readers a direct route into Snorri's mythic system, its gods, its cosmology, and the poetic language that Norse skalds built upon it.
19737-the-principles-of-gothic-ecclesias:
This study explains the principles of Gothic church architecture, with close notes on screen work, arches, shafts, bases, and capitals. Surviving screens at King's Sutton, Cropredy, Beaudesert, and St. John's, Winchester, show the craft in varied states.

A key distinction separates earlier screen work from later work, marked by slender shafts banded midway and arches bearing a flat cornice. The book serves students who want to read a Gothic church by its details, not merely admire its height. The study teaches readers to judge a church by arches, shafts, and screens. The author warns that style changes came so gradually that no precise date ends one style or starts the next.
19853-bob-hunt-in-canada:
George W. Orton wrote Bob Hunt in Canada in 1916 for boy readers. Bob and his friend Bill scheme for a summer outdoors. Bill will work on his father; Bob will get after his. Fathers, Bill notes, already praise open-air life for boys. Their campaign is half won before it starts. Canada means camps, canoes, and game to such heroes.

Orton was an Olympic runner turned author of boys' sports books. His stories prize health, pluck, and clean fun. A Canadian trip gave city boys a wilder stage. The Hunt books made outdoor skill a boy's ambition. Dialogue like this opening moves the plot briskly. It is wholesome adventure from the series-book boom.
21467-the-log-house-by-the-lake-a-tale-o:
A rich English family loses its wealth in court and sails for Canada in W. H. G. Kingston's The Log House by the Lake. They have funds to settle, but not for a grand house. A log house by a lake becomes their new home.

Days pass in sailing and canoeing on the lake in the warm months. Winter freezes the water, and the boys fall into a plight from which they barely escape. Back in England, the cousin who won the case wastes the fortune through bad advice. A surprise ending waits, in a short book of about three hours' reading.
22190-the-stamps-of-canada:
Bertram W. H. Poole wrote The Stamps of Canada as a handbook for collectors. Poole was a tireless philatelic author who catalogued many countries' issues. Canada's stamps began in 1851 with the famous beaver design. From there the Dominion's postal issues grew with the new nation after 1867.

Poole describes each issue, its values, printings, and varieties, in collector's order. He also discusses the stamp albums of his day, sold in five sections so a buyer could choose his branch cheaply. Prices and rarity guide the practical side. The book belongs to the heroic age of stamp collecting, when a handbook like this one could make or break a young collector's cabinet.
22496-the-settlers-in-canada:
Captain Marryat wrote The Settlers in Canada, a tale of emigrant life. Marryat, a naval officer turned novelist, knew the colony well. His settlers must push toward Upper Canada to find their farm.

The land was better in Upper Canada, the account notes. But distance from Quebec and Montreal was much greater there. Populous parts of the colony lay far behind the newcomers. They were left almost wholly to their own resources. Protection, too, was almost wholly lacking on that frontier. Against those odds, a family clears land and builds a life. Marryat gives young readers emigration as adventure. The book also records real hardships British settlers met in Canadian woods.
22557-canada:
Sir J. G. Bourinot wrote Canada, a history in the Story of the Nations series. Bourinot was a Canadian historian and clerk of Parliament. His survey runs from bold French adventurers to Confederation itself.

French settlers first attempted settlement on Annapolis Basin's banks. They also settled the picturesque heights of Quebec in those years. From such beginnings, the story reaches a Confederation spanning a continent. It extends, in his phrase, from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. Along the way come wars, treaties, and rival colonies taking shape. Readers get Canada's national story in one compact, confident volume. It shows how Canadians of Bourinot's generation told their own past.
22942-clare-avery-a-story-of-the-spanish:
Clare Avery, a story of the Spanish Armada, comes with a helpful editorial note. Its author, the note explains, uses many words and phrases now outdated. When such a word first appears, its current meaning is given, as with popinjay, glossed as parrot. Only where a word has reversed its sense, the editor warns, can confusion arise.

Behind that note stands a historical tale of Elizabethan England under threat of invasion. Clare's story plays out as Philip of Spain's great fleet approaches in 1588. The period language is part of the design, dressing the past in its own words. Young readers of the book's day got history, romance, and a vocabulary lesson together. The glosses keep the door open for readers now.
23139-olla-podrida:
A haunted reader opens Olla Podrida. Everything conspires, the narrator says, to remind the sufferer of the one thing he longs to forget. Readers who have never felt it should give thanks, he advises, before sitting down to carve into these pages.

Frederick Marryat named his miscellany after the Spanish stew, a pot of everything. Sketches, tales, and essays jostle in the mixture exactly as promised. The melancholy address to the reader gives the stew its seasoning, a naval author's moods served beside his yarns. Olla Podrida shows Marryat off duty, chopping the whole of his experience into one dish.
23328-esmeralda:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this tale of a French language teacher and his wife, published in the late eighteen seventies. The narrator, a poor teacher, and his wife Clelie, who copies great pictures for small prices, count themselves rich to be together in Paris.

They recall a poorer time in London, apart and struggling, as true calamity. Burnett's story of art, love, and modest means charms by its warmth, and by its portrait of a couple who prize each other above fortune. Esmeralda's mother works new acquaintances as stepping-stones, winning invitations and visits for her daughter.
24211-the-settlers-in-canada:
Captain Marryat wrote this juvenile novel, published in 1844 as the twenty-first book from his pen. Unlike his earlier nautical books, it runs forward in a steady style without the usual asides, with short, even chapters that suit young readers. Its subject is the Canadian wilderness, treated, the producer notes, as well as later masters of the genre.

The story opens in 1791, when an English family goes out to settle in Canada, a province surrendered by the French more than thirty years before. With no steamboats for the rapids, Indians still in Upper and Lower Canada, wild animals abroad, and French settlers displeased at conquest, settling was hard work. Readers get a clear, steady tale of clearing and building a home.
24299-the-cryptogram-a-story-of-northwes:
This adventure novel of northwest Canada was entered for copyright by Street and Smith in the years 1897, 1898, and 1899. Its chapters open with the saving of Gray Moose, a hotel in Bonaventure Street, and Flora Hatherton. Mutual explanations, an alarm in the night, and preparations for flight follow, with the skipper of the Speedwell and a passage at the mercy of the sea.

Later chapters bring a copy of The Times, a warning in woodcraft, an ambuscade, and an Indian's gratitude. Fort Royal, a lost locket, the siege of the house, and the secret of the factor's desk follow. A traveler from Alaska, back from the dead, trunk 409, and the rightful claimant close the tale. Readers get a northern tale of flight, siege, and a secret worked out link by link.
24554-down-south-or-yacht-adventure-in-f:
Oliver Optic wrote this boys' yachting story as the fifth volume of his Great Western series. Earlier volumes took readers west, out west, onto the Great Lakes, and yachting down the Atlantic coast. This one sails to Florida, where a yacht cruise brings adventure in warm waters.

Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, wrote dozens of boys' books mixing travel, work, and pluck. His young sailors learn seamanship, friendship, and fair play as they cruise southern bays and rivers. Young readers get a sunny, old-fashioned adventure, full of boats, ports, and the pleasures of life aboard.
25817-the-cruise-of-the-esmeralda:
Harry Collingwood writes The Cruise of the Esmeralda, a splendid, beautifully written sea tale with a strong nautical background. The hero's family held a long nautical tradition but little money, with a family story of an ancestor's buried treasure.

Centuries before, an ancestor found an abandoned vessel holding gold and jewels, buried it secretly on a Far Eastern island, and hid cipher directions in his English house. The hero finds the cipher paper after long search and sails to find the fortune, undeciphered, facing pirates beaten in a novel manner and further adventures.
30674-famous-firesides-of-french-canada:
Mary Wilson Alloway writes Famous Firesides of French Canada, illustrated and printed in Montreal in 1899 by John Lovell and Son, entered under Canadian copyright that year. An illustration shows hearths beside which were rocked the cradles of those who made Canada's history.

Alloway dedicates the volume by special permission to Lord Strathcona and Mount Royal, chancellor of McGill University and high commissioner for Canada in London. Principal authorities consulted in preparing the work follow the dedication. Alloway tells French Canadian history through famous homes and hearths, linking family, faith, and nation in warm, domestic portraits.
31424-report-of-the-proceedings-at-the-e:
Published at Boston in 1851, this report records the examination of Charles G. Davis, Esq., on a charge of aiding and abetting the rescue of a fugitive slave, held in Boston in February 1851. A prefatory note says the report appears at the request of persons who believed all that was known of the Fugitive Slave Bill in operation should be spread before the public. For lawyers, it adds, the case broke fresh ground in how a statute of major political weight was read and used.

The volume is therefore both a legal record and a political document. It lets readers follow testimony, argument, and procedure in a case that tested the new federal law in a northern courtroom. For students of slavery, abolition, and American law, it preserves a moment when a single prosecution became a public debate about justice and obedience.
31579-olla-podrida:
Captain Marryat's Olla Podrida, published in London by J. M. Dent and Company and in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in 1896, the year given as MDCCCXCVI, is a miscellany of stories and sketches. Its contents include "The Monk of Seville," from the Metropolitan Magazine of 1833, and "The Gipsy" of 1834. They also include "Ill-Will" and three essays on how to write a fashionable novel, a book of travels, and a romance. The title, a Spanish stew of mixed ingredients, suits a volume of varied pieces.

Marryat, the naval novelist, turns his hand here to shorter forms, with humor and observation. The how-to-write pieces satirize literary fashion, while the stories show his range beyond the quarterdeck. Readers of Marryat will find a light, entertaining collection, gathering magazine work that might otherwise have been lost.
3334-drake-s-great-armada:
Captain Walter Biggs tells the story of Drake's great armada in this contemporary account, prepared from a 1910 Collier edition. Nearly five years passed between Drake's return from his famous voyage and the despatch of the formidable armament these pages commemorate. During the last of those years, the introduction notes, events moved remarkably fast.

Gilbert, empowered by Elizabeth, stands among the opening figures, and the expedition to the Spanish Indies follows. Biggs writes as a participant's witness, not a later historian. Readers get Drake's 1585 voyage as his men saw it: a raid on an empire, told in plain, urgent prose, before the Spanish Armada of 1588 fixed Drake's name in legend.
33647-alida:
Alida, or Miscellaneous Sketches of Occurrences during the late American War, is presented twice in this unusual volume. These include first straight, as printed, and then paragraph by paragraph with its sources quoted where known and significant errors of fact noted. The author explains that part of the work was written as a journal of incidents and part to commemorate particular facts for family gratification, never expecting another eye to see it.

A pious friend persuaded the author to allow printing, on condition that proceeds above expenses go to charitable purposes. Contemporary praise quoted in the volume calls the work elegant, poetic, and improving. For modern readers, the double presentation is the treasure. These include a period sketchbook of war and domestic life, paired with a running check on where its stories came from and where they go wrong.
34080-a-historical-geography-of-the-brit:
C. P. Lucas, of Balliol College, Oxford, and the Colonial Office, wrote this history of Canada, volume five of his Historical Geography of the British Colonies, published at Oxford in 1901. Part one treats New France, from European discoverers in North America to the end of the sixteenth century, through Champlain and the founding of Quebec.

Later chapters cover settlement and the Five Nation Indians, French and English down to the Peace of Utrecht, the Mississippi and Louisiana, Acadia and Hudson Bay, Louisbourg, and the conquest of Canada. Appendices list French governors and principal dates to 1763. The book remains a solid imperial history of early Canada.
35008-concerning-belinda:
Concerning Belinda is a set of linked sketches by Eleanor Hoyt Brainerd, with copyright in 1904 and print at New York in 1905. Harrison Fisher and Katharine Richardson drew the pictures. Brainerd opens with an apology to the heads of New York boarding schools for treating their world from its funny side.

The chapters follow Belinda and the girls of her school through small scrapes and young love. Heads promise the musical romance of Amelia, the elopement of Evangeline Marie, and a wolf in the fold. Brainerd admits each school has its earnest pupils, but she writes for the absurd ones, whose follies make the best tales.
35185-the-buddha-s-path-of-virtue-a-tran:
The Buddha Path of Virtue is an English rendering of the Dhammapada by F L Woodward, printed at Madras and London in 1921. Sir Ponnambalam Arunachalam wrote the foreword. The Dhammapada is a core text of Buddhist teaching, set in short verses.

Twenty six parts sort the verses by theme, from The Pairs and Heedfulness to The Mind, Flowers, and Fools. Later parts treat the wise, the self, the world, joy, anger, and craving. The last parts treat the monk and the Brahmana, with a note that Buddhism holds no priesthood of the Western kind. Woodward aims to let English readers walk the path in plain words. Readers of world faiths get a calm, clear guide to right thought and right acts.
37739-egerton-ryerson-and-education-in-u:
Harold Putman's Egerton Ryerson and Education in Upper Canada was published at Toronto in 1912 by William Briggs. Putman inspected public schools at Ottawa and had taught at the Ottawa Normal School. A life of Ryerson comes first, then the school history of the province from 1783 to 1844.

Ryerson was born in 1803 in Charlotteville township, the son of a United Empire Loyalist who had farmed as a pioneer. The boy shared the farm work and read what books he could get. Chapters then follow his reports and bills: the school bill of 1846, the bill of 1850, and the bill of 1871. Separate schools, grammar schools, and the training of teachers each get a full hearing.
40019-the-barren-ground-of-northern-cana:
Warburton Pike wrote this travel book, The Barren Ground of Northern Canada, published at New York in 1917. A preface kept from the first edition opens it with a joke at the author's own cost. In outlying Canada, Pike says, folk believed some kind society in London existed to send incapable men to the ends of the earth for sport.

Strangers asked if he had been sent out by it. They thought less of him when he owned his trip was an ordinary shooting trip, like one to the Rockies or to Africa. His lure was a rumour picked up from Hudson's Bay officers in the northern districts. A strange animal, a relic of an earlier age, still roamed the Barren Ground. That vast desert lies between the bay, the great lakes, and the Arctic Sea. That animal was the musk-ox, known only from native report.
4023-candida:
George Bernard Shaw's comedy sets a clergyman, his wife Candida, and a young poet in a comfortable London suburb on a fine October morning. The Reverend Morell preaches with heartiness, while Eugene Marchbanks, the poet, stares after the household with anxious love.

Candida laughs at the young man's turmoil and asks him what he thinks of her father, turning the play toward its famous choice. Shaw uses wit and debate to test marriage, work, and the romance of being needed. The play remains a bright, talk-driven comedy about who truly holds power in a home.
40526-the-chronicles-of-rhoda:
The Chronicles of Rhoda, a story for young readers by Florence Tinsley Cox, was published at Boston in 1909. Jessie Willcox Smith supplied the illustrations. The book is told by Rhoda herself, a little girl looking back at her childhood. It opens with her grandmother teaching her to say her own name from a catechism.

Chapter titles sketch a child's world of family and neighbours. A Dethroned Queen comes first, then Lily Ann, The Old Major, and The Fireside God. Later chapters bring The Hottentot, A Social Event, Auntie May, and The Green Door. The last is The Hidden Talent. Cox writes in a warm, plain voice suited to her young narrator. The book belongs to a shelf of gentle childhood tales of its day, full of grandparents, lessons, and small adventures seen through a girl's eyes.
4306-veranilda:
George Gissing set this historical novel in Italy during Justinian's long war against the Goths. After seven years of fighting, the great commander Belisarius has returned east with a captive Gothic king. The contents follow Basil, Veranilda, the deacon Leander, the emperor's command, heresy, a snare, and Rome beleaguered.

Gissing, better known for London novels, turns here to late antiquity with care for place and belief. Churchmen, soldiers, and Roman families move through Cumae, Praeneste, and Hadrian's villa. The romance at the center gives the history a human thread, as love and loyalty are tested by war and faith.
43280-jean-baptiste-a-story-of-french-ca:
Jean Baptiste, published in 1915, is a novel of French Canada by Le Rossignol, the author of Little Stories of Quebec. The hero, Jean Baptiste Giroux, grows up in a habitant parish under the eye of his teacher and the parish priest. The opening chapter shows the schoolboy reading aloud the life of Saint John the Baptist, his patron. A long poem by Crémazie on the native shore stands at the front.

The chapters move through village life: a sorcerer, a loup garou, a loan, a robbery and a return. Love, faith and money pull the hero in rival ways. The story gives English readers a warm picture of old Quebec parish life.
4393-wakulla-a-story-of-adventure-in-flo:
Kirk Munroe wrote this boys' adventure of a family's move to Florida, opening with preparations to leave the old home. The schooner Nancy Bell carries them south, with Captain Li's story and a wreck on the Florida reef along the way. Mark and Ruth attend an auction, spend a queer Christmas, and arrive at the new home.

Later chapters bring a Sunday school and more mysteries, a ghost found in a trying position, a runaway's story, and a great mill picnic. The boys fight a forest fire, catch an alligator, and face a fire hunt and an underground river. Munroe's Florida is sunny, strange, and full of incident, told for young readers.
44337-the-lily-and-the-totem-or-the-hugu:
The Lily and the Totem, or The Huguenots in Florida is a historical work by William Gilmore Simms, published in New York by Baker and Scribner in 1850. Simms, author of The Yemassee and lives of Marion and Bayard, dedicates the book to James H Hammond of South Carolina. Its subject is the French colonies of Coligni in North America from 1562 to 1570.

Simms calls the pieces sketches, picturesque and historical. The lily of France and the totem of the native peoples meet in his title. He writes to Hammond of their shared interest in the early history of their state and country. On Southern ground he traces the doubtful progress of the Huguenot settlements. The French Florida colony ended in Spanish massacre, a story Simms tells with a romancer's colour. His history doubles as literature, in the manner of his novels.
44932-free-thought-and-official-propagan:
Free Thought and Official Propaganda is the Conway Memorial Lecture delivered by Bertrand Russell at South Place Institute on March 24, 1922. Graham Wallas sat in the chair, and the lecture was printed in London the same year. Wallas opens the evening by recalling his own forty years as a teacher, and his dismissal thirty-seven years before for refusing religious conformity.

Wallas notes a plain puzzle: after three thousand years of schooling in Europe, students still reach the conclusions of their own nation and school. Most French students end French in outlook, most Americans American, and most Eton boys keep Eton politics for life, though all read newspapers. Russell's lecture takes up the cause: official pressure on what may be taught and thought, and the case for letting evidence rule.
46171-florida-caverns-state-park-mariann:
Florida Caverns is a park guide to the state park at Marianna, Florida, where parties join guides at a stone office near the cave mouth. The office was built by hand from the solid rock base to a roof of hand split cypress shakes. Its walls are of weathered native limestone, held by beams hewn on the ground.

A poem at the front praises wondrous sights of stalactites and stalagmites, a house not made with hands. Fluted columns, pendants from the dome, and sculptured figures large and small fill the verse. The guide says Florida is truly a child of the sea, since all its rocks formed on ocean bottoms or by streams at the shore. The rock record tells how the state rose. Park visitors get the cave tale with its stone formations named.
4736-hadda-pada:
Godmunder Kamban wrote Hadda Padda as a play whose value, its foreword says, lies beneath the surface, in quivering, intensely pulsating forces of life. The speeches breathe, each leading character carries its own melodic theme, and music runs under the text like an accompaniment of exquisite passion. That passion rises, sinks, and rises again, struggling with vacillating sensual pleasure and base inclination to supersede others.

The play opens with olden superstition, in an old nurse's tale about a life-egg, suggested by a crystal ball with which sisters play. Modern superstition weaves into a scene where Hadda Padda, with heroically mastered despair, meets an herborist who talks of plants in calm, poetic manner, recalling Ophelia with her flowers. Readers get an Icelandic drama of passion, poetry, and fate, in a style that prizes atmosphere as much as action.
48246-a-parody-on-princess-ida:
Parody on Princess Ida is a railroad advertising burlesque by Dalziel, editor of the Chicago News Letter. Charlton, passenger agent of the Chicago and Alton Railroad, gave it away with compliments. The scene is the palace of King Alton Hilderbrandt in the city of Chicago. Courtiers, conductors, and passenger agents scan the line for royal Gama with opera glasses.

A chorus searches the panorama for a sign of Gama coming by the Alton. He should arrive this day from Adamant with his daughter and his pal. Gilbert and Sullivan Cambridge girl graduates become a railway joke in the parody. Victorian ephemera keeps few stranger mixes of opera and timetable than this.
48358-a-tour-to-the-river-saguenay-in-lo:
Tour to the River Saguenay is a travel book by Charles Lanman, published in 1848. Carey and Hart of Philadelphia issued the little volume on Lower Canada. Lanman inscribes the book to Solomon Nicoll of New York in testimony of friendship. A dedication letter tells how a fishing dream in May set the tour in motion.

He woke haunted by the idea that he must spend the summer in angling, he writes. Relinquishing editorial labours, he made a pilgrimage that produced this volume of travel. The Saguenay great cliffs and salmon waters draw his sporting pen northward. American travel writing gains a lively early tour of French Canada.
48456-homes-and-careers-in-canada:
Homes and Careers in Canada, by Jeffs, was printed at London in 1914 with sixteen pictures. A publisher's note owns that the sheets were first titled Making Good in Canada until another book took that name. Jeffs counts between 350,000 and 400,000 people a year entering Canada to settle, 60,000 of them from the United States.

Chapters run from why people go, through railway building and settling on the land, to real estate and the homes of Canada. During the season, he says, 10,000 to 15,000 a week sail from Glasgow, Liverpool, Bristol, and Southampton. The frontispiece shows the Parliament Buildings at Ottawa.
48726-diane-of-ville-marie-a-romance-of-:
Diane of Ville Marie, a romance of French Canada, is a historical novel by Blanche Macdonnell, issued at Toronto in 1898. The author dedicates it in loving memory of a mother, who was inspiration, friend, and comforter. Her preface states the tale's errand in plain words. The story tries to make known the men and women who once lived and loved and suffered amid these very scenes, she writes.

In dealing with facts and real persons, she says, it is only fair to tell the reader what liberties have been taken. The Le Ber family were leading figures among their fellows, she then explains. Jacques Le Ber, brother in law to the redoubtable Charles Le Moyne, was one of the richest merchants of New France. A hardy and bold soldier, he was made noble by the French king in 1696.
48845-a-girl-of-the-north-a-story-of-lon:
Helen Milecete wrote A Girl of the North, a story of London and Canada. Greening put out this second edition at London in 1900. Milecete had written A Detached Pirate before this novel. The house stood at 20 Cecil Court, off Charing Cross Road. A list of popular novels from the same shelves fronts the book.

Prices there run from half a crown to six shillings a volume. The tale itself runs through sixteen chapters and more in plain number order. Its ground is named in the subtitle: the great city and the northern dominion. A girl of the north stands at the heart of that double setting. One man in the cast is marked for unusual talent and power, the notices say. He had translated the newest book of a famed Danish naturalist. Milecete gives a romance of two worlds at the century's turn.
49493-leda:
Aldous Huxley published a book of poems with the New York firm of Doran, after his first book Limbo. The title poem, Leda, retells the Greek myth in rich verse. It opens on the river Eurotas, brown and bright as an agate, slipping from pool to pool through pines, chestnut groves, and terraced vines to a soundless bay.

In the deep pools men fancy they see shining hair and pale bodies, ghosts of old beauty. Shorter poems follow on Jonah, a melody by Scarlatti, sunsets, fatigue, and a merry go round. Songs of philosophers and pieces on art, beauty, and last things fill the small book. Young Huxley's wit and love of fine sound mark every page.
49763-peeps-at-many-lands-canada:
Peeps at Many Lands: Canada is a young readers' survey of the Dominion by Bealby, published by Adam and Charles Black at London in 1909. Twelve full-page color pictures by six artists fill the book. The frontispiece shows a family ready for a sleigh ride, and a sketch map opens the text.

Sixteen chapters tour the country. They take in the far west, home life, winter sports, and fifty below zero. Law and order, the ship of the prairie, golden wheat, and timber follow. Later chapters treat rock and sand wealth, waterways, the Iroquois wars, the habitant of the St. Lawrence shore, and the home of Evangeline.
49968-fort-jefferson-national-monument-f:
Fort Jefferson National Monument, Florida, describes the great sea fort on Garden Key in the Dry Tortugas, almost 70 miles west of Key West in the Gulf of Mexico. Fort Jefferson, built from 1846 to 1874, was the largest of the nineteenth century American coastal forts, once called the key to the Gulf of Mexico.

Ponce de Leon named the islands las Tortugas in 1513, for the turtles that bred there; the later word Dry warns that no fresh water is found. A lighthouse rose on Garden Key in 1825; the present 150 foot light stands on Loggerhead Key. The fort covers most of its 16 acre key. Its walls, 8 feet thick, stand 50 feet high in three gun tiers, designed for 450 guns and a garrison of 1500 men. Work ran nearly 30 years and the fort was never finished.
50449-recruit-for-andromeda:
Recruit for Andromeda is a science fiction novel by Milton Lesser. Ace Books of New York issued the novel in nineteen fifty nine. Its cover tale, Tournament Under Nightmare Skies, sets the hook for readers. Kit Temple is drafted for the Nowhere Journey in that tale.

Men called for that flight are promised rotation, yet none ever return. Kit fellow draftee Arkalion, with strange old man eyes, seems to know more. Kit twists fate and follows him to the ends of space and time. There he finds the secret of Nowhere and a test for Earth future. Chapter one opens with riots in Center City in May sunlight.
50569-herakles-the-hero-of-thebes-and-ot:
Herakles the Hero of Thebes and Other Heroes of the Myth is a school book of Greek myth, printed by Scribner at New York in 1900. Mary Burt and Zénaïde Ragozin adapted it from the second book of the primary schools of Athens. A pronunciation guide closes the volume. The book belongs to Scribner's series of school reading.

Burt taught in a New York school and edited story books for children. Ragozin had written the stories of Chaldea and Assyria and belonged to learned societies on three sides of the Atlantic. Their Herakles brings the strong man of Thebes and his fellow heroes to American classrooms in the very words, sifted, of a Greek school text. The adaptation is a small bridge between two schoolrooms, ancient matter in modern use.
50899-mam-linda:
Mam' Linda is a novel by Will Harben, published in 1907 with illustrations by F B Masters. The first chapter opens in a southern country store. At the back, under a hanging lamp, four young men play poker at a round table. Near the door the storekeeper, James Blackburn, talks with Carson Dwight, a young lawyer of the town. Blackburn is forty-five, portly and bearded, and young at heart. He will not hear that he grumbles at the boys, he says.

The talk shows Blackburn's soft spot: the young men treat him as one of their own. Marriage has not tamed his love of devilment, Dwight tells him, and the crowd loves to hang round the store for it. Harben wrote of Georgia folk and their small towns. The novel builds its tale on this store, its poker crowd, and the Black woman whose name it bears.
51642-lucinda:
Lucinda is a novel by Hope, author of the famed tale of a held king in a small land of the hills. It came out at Toronto in the first years past the great war, printed in America. Its rights were held that year by its hand in full name.

Its parts run like a gay hunt of love and plot. A face in a cab, a sign, and a great blast open the tale. A fourth hand, a catch who catch can game, and a trip to the queen of the seas fill the next run. Self guard, a needle wife, and like to like lead to her ladyship. A queer word for a great house scheme of state marks the mid point of the book.
52034-the-coming-night-a-sermon-preached:
The Coming Night is a funeral sermon by the Reverend Edward Hoare. Thomas Hatchard issued it at London in 1857 from the preached text. Hoare preached it in Cromer Church on Friday, June 12, 1857, he notes. The occasion was the death of Anna Gurney of Northrepps Cottage nearby.

His text is John chapter nine, verse four: the night cometh, when no man can work. Gurney had stood foremost in large hearted Christian benevolence for years there. The poor lost a kind friend; children lost a devoted teacher in her. Hoare likens her passing to Lazarus death at Bethany in the gospel. Sorrow, he argues, serves a wise unseen purpose in the sight of God.
52290-studies-in-the-south-and-west-with:
Studies in the South and West, with Comments on Canada, is a travel book by Charles Dudley Warner, printed at New York in 1889. The studies were undertaken at the suggestion of Henry M Alden, editor of Harper's Monthly, and most of them passed under his eye. Their object was not a comprehensive account of the country.

Warner aimed to note representative developments, tendencies, and dispositions, so as to lead to a better understanding between different sections. The papers give impressions of the South in 1885 and society in the New South. New Orleans, a voudou dance, and the Acadian land follow. The South revisited in 1887, Minnesota and Wisconsin, and two papers on Chicago come next. Three capitals, Cincinnati and Louisville, Memphis and Little Rock, and Kentucky fill the western half. Comments on Canada close the book. Warner confesses that hospitality may have coloured his brief sojourn's opinions.
52702-mrs-peixada:
Mrs Peixada is a novel by Henry Harland, writing as Sidney Luska, published by Cassell in New York in 1886. Harland was already known for As It Was Written. The story is told in twelve chapters with teasing titles, from A Case Is Stated to How She Endeavored to Explain Her Life. The title figure enters only in the seventh chapter, after much groundwork.

The book opens on April 25, a date the young lawyer Arthur Ripley will always mark. That morning he pocketed his first serious retainer. Reaching his office late after a walk in fine weather, he finds the brewer Mendel waiting with two strangers. Mendel fires personal questions at a family friend, the lawyer Vail, about his mother and his unmarried state. The scene sets the novel's world of New York business, law, and family pressure, into which Mrs Peixada will step.
53243-historical-sketches-of-colonial-fl:
Richard Campbell wrote these sketches of colonial Florida to fill a gap, since no history of British rule in West Florida existed. The Williams Publishing Company of Cleveland printed the book in 1892. Campbell drew on original records in the Archives of Canada, pointed out to him by William Kingsford of Ottawa. An account of British rule, he says, required one of the Spanish annals before and after it.

The Creeks get much space because the body of that nation lived inside British West Florida for twenty years. Their British ties shaped their conduct toward the United States until after 1812. The life of Alexander McGillivray is part of that story. Pensacola stands at the center as capital of both British and Spanish West Florida, and the opening chapters follow the discovery of its bay and the first settlement under Luna.
53608-the-history-of-saint-augustine-flo:
The History of Saint Augustine, Florida is a work by Dewhurst, printed at New York in 1881. Its opening account treats the early Spanish and French attempts at settlement in Florida. Sketches follow of events and objects tied to the oldest town in the United States. A short account of the climate and merits of Saint Augustine as a health resort is added at the end.

In his preface Dewhurst says he has boiled down the long accounts of early writers for the general reader. He keeps their quaint language where it suits the place, and draws on traditions held by descendants of the first settlers. He names De Soto's narrator, Cabeza de Vaca, and Bartram among his sources.
54535-the-changed-valentines-and-other-p:
Elizabeth Guptill wrote these plays for St Valentine's Day for Baker's Edition of Plays at Boston. The book sold for twenty-five cents and was copyrighted in 1917. Three plays fill it. The Changed Valentines takes three males and four females. A Romance of St Valentine's Day takes one male and two females. The Queen of Hearts needs eleven males and thirteen females, a whole schoolroom of hearts.

The first play opens in a family living-room. Bert sits at a desk finishing a note to tuck in with a valentine, addressed to Eloise Worthington. A pretty name, and a stately one, he muses, but somehow he likes Winston better, his family name, shared with his sisters Evelyn, Helen, and Louise and his small brother Bobby. Their bachelor uncle completes the cast. Baker's amateur plays were built for parlor and school stages, with scenery kept simple and sentiments kept sweet.
56800-romantic-canada:
Victoria Hayward traveled her own country and wrote it up for Macmillan of Canada in 1922. Edith Watson took the photographs. The publisher's foreword calls the book a truly outstanding work of travel. The chapters begin in Nova Scotia, among barrels, longshoremen, and sea coast homes. Low tide in the Bay of Fundy and Cape Breton follow.

Newfoundland, Labrador, and the French islands come next. Quebec fills a long stretch, with wayside crosses, garden shrines, wood carving, and basket makers. Ontario and the prairie carry the road west. Winnipeg, the Mennonites, and The Pas, gate of the north, have chapters of their own. British Columbia closes the book, with the Doukhobors, the salmon town of Steveston, and the Indians of Alert Bay. Hayward hunts the romance that clings to workaday Canada, in nets, looms, and shrines.
57764-crimes-of-preachers-in-the-united-:
The Truth Seeker Company of New York gathered this grim catalogue from the newspapers of its day. Crimes of Preachers in the United States and Canada reached a tenth edition. Its lines from the Bible stand as a taunt: these be thy gods, O Israel; by their fruits shall ye know them.

The book opens with a wager from 1906. The Pittsburgh YMCA had barred an actor as unfit in morals. Henry Dixey, a famed actor, put up a thousand dollars for charity. If any man could show actors were worse, man for man, than ministers, the money was his. No champion of the cloth claimed it. Case by printed case, the book lists thefts, frauds, and worse by men of the pulpit.
58849-steam-navigation-and-its-relation-:
Steam Navigation and Its Relation to the Commerce of Canada is a trade study. James Croil of Montreal wrote it, with plates and faces of chiefs. The book is given to the chief of the realm in those years. Three lords of the rail and sea world stand at its front.

Croil asks how the steam boat changed the trade of the young realm. Ports, lakes, and streams of the north are the scene of his facts. The tale of steam on those waves is told from its first boats. What steam did for the sale of wheat, wood, and ore is weighed in turn. The link of the realm to the States by water gets its own care. The book is a proud count of the realm's growth by steam and sail.
59220-trail-tales-of-western-canada:
Trail-Tales of Western Canada, by F A Robinson, was published by Marshall Brothers of London in nineteen fourteen. A preface letter dated at Winnipeg that October opens the volume. The tales are set in the mining camps, lumber camps, and bush country of British Columbia and the western provinces.

The contents list stories such as Old Ken's Round-up, The Banner Mines, The Cookee, The Snake-room, The Bush Fire, and Ruth and the Prodigal. The opening tale follows Old Ken, an aging prospector who spent fifty years drinking in a rough camp. Men there said glibly that there was no God west of the Rockies. Yet no man in camp was more popular than Old Ken. Photographs of shacks, mines, coke ovens, and camp kitchens fill the plate list. The book records frontier work camps at the moment they were passing away.
61973-the-giant-fish-of-florida:
The Giant Fish of Florida is a book of sport with rod and line by J. Turner-Turner, put out at London and in the chief town of the Quaker state in nineteen hundred and two. It holds eight and forty plates in all. The first words were signed from a club of horse men at the Yule of the year past. The list of parts reads like a log of the wild coast of that south state.

The giant tarpon heads the book, with a full part on how to catch that great fish. Then come hunts past the great snap beasts of the swamps, and wild hours in the pass. Women who love the sport have a part of their own.
62154-canada:
Beckles Willson wrote a romance of empire on Canada, issued in London in 1907 with twelve coloured plates by Henry Sandham. The book is dedicated to his son Gordon. Its first chapter shows Cartier raising the flag of the lilies, and the tale runs from there to his own day.

Chapters tell of Champlain, the founding of Montreal, and the fury of the Iroquois. Louisburg falls and is given back, the Acadians are banished, and Wolfe takes Quebec. The coming of the Loyalists and the defence against later foes close the story. Willson writes history as high romance, with heroes, flags, and fights at every turn of the road.
62496-the-ra-ma-yana-volume-4-uttara-ka-:
Volume 4 of the Ramayana in English prose holds the Uttara Kanda, the last book of the epic. The rendering was made from the Sanskrit of Valmiki. It was edited and put out by Manmatha Nath Dutt at Calcutta in 1894. The text was made from page pictures of the first print held by the Internet Archive, from two scans of the work.

A note by the transcriber states the rules of the text. Words in italics in this form were set in italics in the first print. Clear slips in spelling have been set right, but shifts in spelling have been let stand. The contents list the sections of the Uttara Kanda in a long run, by number. The volume is the close of a full prose rendering of the great Sanskrit epic.
63152-sir-george-arthur-and-his-administ:
Walter Sage wrote this study of Sir George Arthur and his administration of Upper Canada. It appeared in the bulletin of the history and political science departments at Queen's University, Kingston. The study is number 28 of the series, dated July 1918.

Sage begins with a reputation. Arthur was the last lieutenant-governor of Upper Canada before the Union of 1841. To most Canadians he is little more than a name. He lacked the colour of his predecessor, Sir Francis Bond Head. But he holds his place in history for two acts. He refused to reprieve Lount and Matthews, the rebels of 1837. And he made common cause with the Family Compact against the Reformers. His real term ran barely 18 months, from March 1838 to November 1839. He arrived with Mackenzie's rebellion just crushed. Canadian readers get the hanging governor weighed by a university historian.
63159-treasure-of-the-brasada:
Treasure of the Brasada is a Western novel by Les Savage Junior, copyrighted in 1947 and reprinted by Dell, subtitled peril and intrigue on the border. The brasada is the wild brush country between Texas and Mexico. Before the story starts, the book prints a cast list in the pulp manner, each person sketched in a burning paragraph.

Glenn Crawford, the hero, comes out of hospital after an accident he suspects was planned, racked by panic whenever he nears a horse. Around him gather Merida Lopez, a mysterious beauty, and Dr Huerta, who studies Crawford's symptoms. Old Delcazar fears his friend is mixed in the most dangerous thing that ever hit the brush country.
64191-the-seminoles-of-florida:
Minnie Moore-Willson wrote this account of the Seminoles of Florida. Moffat, Yard printed the seventh edition in New York in 1920. A photo of Hoke-ti-chee, little girl with bright eyes, fronts it. The book is given to Elizabeth Stauffer-Moore for her aid work.

Part one tells facts of the earlier days and removal efforts. Massacre of Thompson and Dade forces and a dishonored treaty follow. Osceola, the rising sun, his capture, and a hidden war camp appear. Part two treats present condition and friends of the Seminoles. Chieftain Tallahassee stands in the later contents of the Florida Seminole account.
64511-black-priestess-of-varda:
Erik Fennel wrote Black Priestess of Varda, a science fiction tale printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1947. The head line names the witch: Sin, foul priestess and raving beauty, beloved of Sasso, the Dark Power who strives to capture a lovely little world with her help. Their only fear is a whispered legend, Elvedon the Savior.

The tale opens far from Varda, in a shadowed laboratory. Eldon Carmichael writes a letter to Margaret with his right hand, clumsily, having been left-handed before his injury. He remembers his first one-eyed look in a mirror after the bandages came off. A wrench slipped from Victor Schenley's hand, he recalls, into the Institute's great compressor. The blurb's joke waits behind the scene: this crippled man, blundering through a shower of sparks into another time, cannot be Elvedon, can he?
65072-the-time-armada:
The Time Armada is a science fiction novel by Fox B Holden, printed in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in October and November 1953. The magazine text is the source of this edition.

The story opens on a rainy April afternoon in 1958. Congressman Douglas Blair, once a physicist, rides through Washington traffic with the reporter Carl Grayson. Blair is worn down by the McKenny bill, a measure pushed by a clever rival who holds the steel men in his hand. McKenny has said openly that the people have no say in government and never did. That scorn, and Blair's double life in politics and science, set the tale moving. The cover lines promise that this beginning has its end worlds away.
65750-life-in-canada:
Life in Canada is a memoir and history by Thomas Conant, printed at Toronto in 1903. Conant also wrote Upper Canada Sketches. His account covers a hundred years, from October 1792. On that date his ancestor Roger Conant, a Yale graduate, landed in Canada as a United Empire Loyalist. Roger had owned land in Massachusetts before the move. Family papers and tales passed down father to son form the book's store.

Conant calls those plain statements a trust he owes the public. Future historians, he argues, will find their best materials in such records. He writes chiefly of Ontario, where his family always lived. He is careful to honour the other provinces as well. The Canada of his day held five and a third million people. He foresaw a far larger nation eager for its early history. The book preserves the manners and customs of that first century.
69330-life-of-sir-walter-scott-with-abbo:
Life of Sir Walter Scott is a biography by Robert Chambers. Robert Carruthers added notes on Abbotsford, Scott's home. Chambers and Company published the edition at Edinburgh and London in 1871. A prefatory note by the editor, William Chambers, explains the book. His brother wrote the memoir just after the novelist's death. It was issued at a small price for popular reading. It had a large circulation, some 180,000 copies in all.

The memoir is now reproduced in somewhat better style, the note says. The occasion is the centenary of Scott's birth in August 1871. The editor added only a few paragraphs in brackets. One insertion tells how his brother came to know Scott. The frontispiece shows Abbotsford and its grounds from the Tweed. The book gives general readers a life of the great novelist. The added notes root that life in his famous house.
70425-narrative-of-the-fenian-invasion-o:
Alexander Somerville wrote a Narrative of the Fenian Invasion of Canada, published for the author at Hamilton, Canada West, by Joseph Lyght in eighteen sixty six. A map of the field of combat at Limestone Ridge aids the text. Somerville tells the raid as a witness and a Canadian. The book opens with politics, a speech by Lord John Russell in eighteen forty four. Irish grievance frames the invasion tale.

On February fourteenth, eighteen forty four, Sir Robert Peel told Parliament that a commission of inquiry would go to Ireland. Lord John Russell, leader of the opposition, then spoke words Somerville quotes at length. The narrative then treats the Fenian brotherhood, its American camps, and the crossing into Canada. Battles at Limestone Ridge and Fort Erie fill the centre. Canadian volunteers, prisoners, and courts martial close the tale. Historians get a near contemporary account of the eighteen sixty six raid.
73533-the-poetic-edda:
The Poetic Edda, turned into English by Henry Adams Bellows, was published in New York in 1923. Two volumes are bound in one here. The American-Scandinavian Foundation issued it in its classics line. Bellows adds an introduction and notes. The poems split into lays of the gods and lays of the heroes. Voluspo and Hovamol open the god lays. The flyting of Loki and the lay of Thrym follow. Rigsthula and the dream of Baldr close that part.

Hero lays tell of Volund, Helgi, and Sigurd the dragon slayer. Guthrun's grief fills many later lays. Atli and the Niflungs bring the set to its grim end. Bellows notes that the poems lived by mouth for ages before writing. Their dates and homes stay in dispute, he says.
7469-daniel-deronda:
George Eliot's last novel opens near four o'clock on a September day, in a haze of gambling-room stillness broken by the rattle and chink of the tables. Gwendolen Harleth, the spoiled child of the first book, is at the center of that scene, beautiful, willful, and already gambling with her future. Daniel Deronda, watching her, becomes the other pole of the story.

The novel follows two streams toward a meeting. One is Gwendolen's choice of marriage and its consequences. The other is Deronda's search for his origins, which leads him to Mordecai and to a vision of Jewish national life. Books titled Maidens Choosing, Mordecai, Revelations, and Fruit and Seed mark the journey. Daniel Deronda is Eliot's most ambitious novel, joining a marriage plot to a profound inquiry into identity and belonging.
75178-across-the-sub-arctics-of-canada:
Across the Sub-Arctics of Canada tells of a journey of 3,200 miles by canoe and snowshoe through the Barren Lands. Dodd, Mead and Company published Tyrrell's account at New York in 1898, with drawings by Arthur Heming and photographs taken on the way. The frontispiece shows the author in Eskimo costume.

The route runs from Toronto to Athabasca Landing, down the Athabasca and past Fort Chipewyan to Black Lake, then into unknown wilderness. Chapters follow the Telzoa River, the home of the reindeer, meetings with natives and the customs of the Eskimos, polar bears, and Fort Churchill. Appendices add the plants collected, a vocabulary of Eskimo words, a route map and a classified index.
77708-wanda:
Przyiemski wrote this dramatic poem on Wanda, queen of old Poland. A translator rendered it in English, privately printed in 1863. A Schiller verse on seed hid in earth heads the poem. The front note says early Polish history is little known in England.

Wanda, daughter of the founder of Cracow, gave her life for her land. The poem casts her maidens Lesja, Halina, and Rzewna near her. Leszek, a Polish officer, and Hermann, an envoy, fill the cast. Choruses of maidens, warriors, folk, goblins, and water spirits sing throughout. The poem was printed in private in 1863.
78634-propaganda:
Propaganda is a trade of minds book by Edward Bernays, out in nineteen twenty eight. A Liveright house of New York brought it out that year in full. Bernays wrote Crystallizing Public Opinion in a past book of like theme. He gives this book to his wife Doris Fleischman in its front leaves. Part one, called Organizing Chaos, heads the scheme of the book.

Keen steer of mass ways and views is a key part of free rule, it opens. A hid state of men we never hear of rules us, that part holds. Our minds are cast and our tastes formed by those few hands there. New hands at the craft, crowd mind lore, and trade ties fill mid parts. Women work, school, alms, art, and the tools of the craft close the scheme.
79305-the-boer-concentration-camps-of-be:
The Boer Concentration Camps of Bermuda, by John Hassell, gives a first hand check on British press claims. Hassell had served as a captain of American scouts in the Boer army. British papers had praised the health of the Bermuda camps and the kind treatment of Boer prisoners held there. One paper even said many prisoners wished to go back and aid the King soldiers.

Those reports reached American papers and stirred doubt among friends of the Boers in New York. A young Boer who escaped and reached New York told a far darker tale of camp life. Friends in the city asked Hassell to learn the truth in person on the ground. He agreed to the task, armed with a passport, and sailed from New York. His book sets out what that mission set out to test.
9455-tales-and-novels-volume-03-belinda:
Maria Edgeworth's third volume of Tales and Novels gives Belinda, in an 1857 printing with engravings on steel. Contents run from characters and masks, through Lady Delacour's history and birthday dresses, to the serpentine river and a family party. Advice, a mysterious boudoir, and difficulties follow, with a macaw and sortes Virgilianae.

Mrs. Stanhope, skilled in the art of rising in the world, launches Belinda into society with small fortune. Edgeworth satirizes fashion, jealousy, and the rights of woman with wit. The novel remains a sparkling comedy of manners, and a feminist landmark of its age.
95-the-prisoner-of-zenda:
Rudolf Rassendyll, an English gentleman on holiday, looks exactly like the king of Ruritania. Anthony Hope's Prisoner of Zenda turns that likeness into a rescue plot when the king is drugged and locked in Zenda castle. Rassendyll must play king at the coronation.

Princess Flavia loves the stand-in, while Black Michael and Rupert of Hentzau plot murder. A cellar secret, a tea-table trick, and a forest duel raise the stakes. The novel ends with duty beating love, as Rassendyll leaves Ruritania. It founded the Ruritanian romance. Hope's Ruritania inspired operettas, films, and a whole shelf of imitation kingdoms.
9968-the-young-woodsman-or-life-in-the-f:
J. Macdonald Oxley's 1895 boys' book follows a young man who answers the call to work in the Canadian lumber woods. He chooses his occupation, travels to the woods, builds a shanty, and learns to keep a standing fire through the cold.

Life in the lumber camp brings a thrilling experience, a rescue in the nick of time, a hunting trip, and the great spring drive, when logs ride the rivers home. Oxley writes with firsthand feeling for axes, snow, and camp fellowship. Young readers get a sturdy tale of work, courage, and the Canadian forest.
atlantida:
Pierre Benoit's Sahara romance appears here in the Ace Books translation by Mary C. Tongue and Mary Ross. A frame letter, dated at Hassi-Inifel in November 1903, explains that Lieutenant Ferrieres left his manuscript sealed before departing for the Tassili of the Tuareg. Plato's Critias stands as epigraph, hinting where the buried secret lies.

Narrator Morhange and his companion reach a hidden city inside the central Sahara, ruled from a mysterious hall with a splashing fountain. Professor Le Mesge presides while Tuareg servants unwrap a rigid human form before the horrified visitors. Benoit builds his lost Atlantis out of classical myth, colonial soldiering, and gothic dread: a queen's palace under the desert, stocked with the preserved lovers who reached it before.
britannica-1911-ababda:
Abābda receives a tribal entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed by Thomas Athol Joyce. The Abābda, nomads of Hamitic stock who call themselves sons of the Jinns, range from the Nile at Assuan to the Red Sea. Pliny's Gebadei and the old Blemmyes stand behind them in the record.

Caravan guides and pilgrim escorts were their old trade, and telegraph work is a new one. An hereditary chief rules some 30,000 in Egypt, paid a subsidy to guard travellers rather than paying tribute. Huts of hurdles and mats, not tents, house them, and camels carry their loads. Milk and durra form the diet. Russegger counted 40,000 in Nubia in 1836, since shrunk by merger with the Bisharin. Dress, speech, and custom fill the close.
britannica-1911-abulfeda:
Abulfeda (1273-1331) was an Arabian historian and geographer born at Damascus, a descendant of Ayyub, father of Saladin. From his twelfth year he was almost constantly on military expeditions against the crusaders, fighting at Tripoli and Acre. Service under the Mameluke sultan brought him the governorship of Hamah, then the rank of prince, and finally hereditary sultan.

Rule gave him time to write. His Abridgment of the History of the Human Race runs in annals from the creation of the world to 1329. His Geography follows earlier writers back to Ptolemy, with twenty-eight sections tabulating the chief towns of the world, their positions, spellings, and notes drawn from earlier authors.
britannica-1911-adda:
Adda is a river of northern Italy. Its ancient name was Addua. Small lakes near the Fraele glen form its source. Streams near Bormio swell its volume considerably. It flows south-west, then due west. The fertile Valtellina valley carries its upper course. Tirano and Sondrio stand along its banks. Tributaries Poschiavino and Malero join it there. The river falls into Lake Como's northern end. It mainly forms that famous lake.

Lombardy's plain takes its lower course. Issuing from Como's Lecco arm, it crosses the plain. After about one hundred and fifty miles it joins the Po. The junction lies eight miles above Cremona. Venice and Milan once bordered along its lower banks. Napoleon defeated the Austrians at Lodi on its banks in 1796.
britannica-1911-alameda:
Alameda is a city of homes in Alameda county, California. It stands on a made island about five miles long and one mile wide, on the east side of San Francisco bay. It faces San Francisco, about six miles off, and lies just south of Oakland. A drain canal, crossed by bridges, parts it from Oakland. Bay Farm island, of about three square miles, lies in the bounds of the city as well. Its people numbered 16,464 in 1900 and 23,383 in 1910.

The Southern Pacific railway serves Alameda, and a tram line links it with Oakland and Berkeley. Its site is low and flat, and its plan is fair and straight. Its works make tiles of baked clay, pottery, rugs, cooling boxes, and salt. The city owns and runs its own plant for electric light.
britannica-1911-alhama-de-granada:
Alhama de Granada, a town of southern Spain, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Granada, twenty-four miles south-west of the city of Granada, and held 7,679 people in 1900. The town sits finely on a ledge of rock above a deep gorge cut by the river Marchan. Behind it the Sierra de Alhama rises to 6,800 feet.

Much of the town is modern for a painful reason. An earthquake in 1884 destroyed over a thousand picturesque old Moorish houses, five churches, the hospital, the theatre, and the prison, and killed 800 inhabitants. Subscriptions came from all Spain, and the town was rebuilt a little distance away. The baths that give Alhama its name, Arabic for the Bath, survived by the river. Their hot sulphurous springs, used since Roman times, draw visitors in spring and autumn for rheumatism and dyspepsia, and for the district's fine scenery.
britannica-1911-almeida:
Spain took Almeida's fortress in 1762, and harder fighting came in the Peninsular War. French troops seized the place in 1810; the next year allied British and Portuguese forces under Lord Wellington won it back. First his men beat Marshal Masséna's relief force at Fuentes de Oñoro on 5 May 1811, and five days later the fortress itself fell.

Almeida stands in hilly country in north-eastern Portugal, in the district of Guarda and once in the province of Beira. Two rivers frame it: the Côa, a tributary of the Douro, and the Turones, a branch of the Agueda. Its people numbered 2,330 in 1900. For long years it ranked among Portugal's chief frontier strongholds facing Spain, and the ground between the Coa and Ciudad Rodrigo saw heavy fighting.
britannica-1911-annelida:
Annelida is a beast entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a major group of worms whose bodies are built in rings. The worms hold a gut that runs through a true body space. Fine bristles set in pits of the skin help them move and grip.

The entry sets out the shared plan of the whole worm group in detail. A head end bears sense tools, and a nerve chain runs the length of the trunk. Blood flows in a closed set of tubes through the rings. Waste leaves by small paired tubes in each ring of the body. Three subgroups of the worms are named at the close of the survey.
britannica-1911-arthropoda:
Arthropoda, a great group of animals with jointed limbs, is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name points to the jointing of the hard outer shell on their limbs and side appendages. The group covers, roughly, crustaceans, spiders and their kin, true insects, centipedes, and millipedes. Siebold and Stannius first used the word in classification in 1845.

The entry traces how the group was carved out of older schemes of life. Cuvier had placed these animals in a broad branch called Articulata, with the ringed worms. When the worms were set apart, the jointed limb animals stood as a group of their own. Other names, such as Condylopoda and Gnathopoda, were later put forward for the same group. Late work in the 1800s then broke up the old catch all group of Vermes.
britannica-1911-asafetida:
Asafetida is a drug article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Asafetida is a gum-resin with a famously foul smell. Its name joins a Persian word for mastic with a Latin word meaning stinking. It is drawn chiefly from the root of the plant Ferula fetida.

The plant grows in eastern Persia and Afghanistan, with Herat and Kandahar as trade centres. It stands five to six feet tall when full grown. At four years of age the plant is ready to yield its resin. The stems are then cut down close to the root. Juice flows out from the cut and hardens into the drug of commerce. The entry also sets the substance apart from a prized ancient drug of a similar name. Readers learn what asafetida is, where it grows, and how the harvest is taken.
britannica-1911-bahya-ibn-paquda:
Bahya ibn Paquda was a Jewish ethical writer who flourished at Saragossa in the 11th century. In 1040 he wrote, in Arabic, a treatise called Duties of the Heart, counted among the most significant and influential Jewish works of the middle ages.

Bahya pictures religion as an intensely spiritual thing, rising at times to passionate mysticism, while still reverencing the Law in the rabbinical sense and folding it into the Jew's inner life. His book falls in ten parts: God's unity, contemplation, worship, trust, consecration, humility, repentance, self-examination, the ascetic life, and the love of God. Selections reached English readers through E. Collins's translation, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-banda:
Banda is a town and district of British India, in the Allahabad division of the United Provinces. The town stands near the right bank of the river Ken, 95 miles south-west of Allahabad, and held 22,565 people in 1901. It counted 65 mosques and 168 Hindu temples, and it was once, but by then no longer, a military cantonment.

The district covers 3,061 square miles and is called the most barren and backward part of the province. Granite uplands, marshy lowlands that flood in the rains, and ravines along the Jumna mark its ground. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the district population as 631,058 in 1901, down eleven per cent in ten years from famine. Its black soil grows millet, rice, cotton, and oil seeds.
britannica-1911-baroda:
Baroda is a native state of India, in direct relations with the governor-general. It is made up of four isolated divisions. They are tangled in the most intricate fashion with British territory and other native states. Three divisions, Kadi, Baroda, and Nausari, lie in Gujarat proper; the fourth, Amreli with Okhamandal, lies in the Kathiawar peninsula. The whole covers 8,099 square miles.

Its population in 1901 was 1,952,692, down nineteen per cent in ten years. The entry lays that fall to the famines of 1896–1897 and 1900–1901. Cholera and fever came with the famines, and plague struck too. The princes of Baroda were a chief branch of the Mahratta confederacy. The 1911 Britannica entry opens their history with Pilaji Gaekwar, who carved out his Gujarat territory about 1721.
britannica-1911-benda:
Benda is the name of a family of German musicians, chief among them Georg Benda (died 1795). Georg learned from his elder brother Franz, concertmaster in Berlin, and won fame as a player of the clavier and the oboe. His lasting place in music history, though, rests on his melodramas.

Melodrama here means spoken words carried by descriptive music, and Benda, a far solider musician than Rousseau, pioneered the form. His Ariadne auf Naxos of 1774 set it going after his Italian trip. Mozart caught fire from it in 1778, carried Ariadne and Medea about with him, and tried the manner himself in his unfinished Zäide of 1780.
britannica-1911-bida:
Bida is a town and district in the British protectorate of Northern Nigeria. The town stands at 9 degrees 5 minutes north and 6 degrees east. It is the capital of the province of Nupe. Fula rule founded it in 1859, and it is walled and of good size. In 1909 a railway joined it to Baro on the Niger, 40 miles away. Its people, mostly Hausa, trade widely from the town.

The 1911 Britannica entry praises Bida's craft work above all. Its embossed brass and copper ware is famous, and its goblets blend the two metals with elegant design. A glass factory, indigo making, and cloth dyeing also flourish. Huge shade trees make the town look like a forest from afar. The article recalls the 1897 fight with the Royal Niger Company. Since British control the town has been quiet and prosperous.
britannica-1911-bischofswerda:
Bischofswerda is a German town in the kingdom of Saxony, on the Wesenitz river. It sits in the governmental district of Bautzen. Two railways meet there, the Dresden to Görlitz line and the Bischofswerda to Zittau line. Its population in 1905 was 7,465. Cloth, artificial flowers, and cigars are made in its factories. Glass-works and potteries also work in the town. Large granite quarries lie in the ground nearby.

The town is famous as the scene of a battle on 12 May 1813. French and Allied forces fought there after Napoleon's retreat from Moscow, the 1911 Britannica entry says. In the 11th century Benno, bishop of Meissen, had his residence in the town. The Bishop's Road still runs from Bischofswerda to Meissen in his memory. The entry is a compact gazetteer note, with industry and the 1813 fight as its two main points. No churches or rulers are named in the text.
britannica-1911-blida:
Blida is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town of Algeria. Blida lies thirty-two miles south west of Algiers by rail, at the base of the Little Atlas. Its population in 1906 was 16,866. The river beside it drives large corn mills and factories and fills the town's many fountains and watered gardens.

The article describes the town and its trade. A long wall with six gates surrounds it, and Fort Mimieh crowns a hill across the river. The modern town, French in character, has arcaded streets, mosques and churches, barracks and a large military hospital. Blida trades chiefly in oranges and flour; its groves hold over fifty thousand orange trees, and cork and cedar add to its wealth.
britannica-1911-bologna-giovanni-da:
Giovanni da Bologna (1524–1608), whose real name was Jean Bologne, was a French sculptor who made his career in Italy. Born at Douai, he trained at Antwerp, went south at twenty-five, and settled in Florence in 1553. Most of his best work still stands in that city.

Two works made his name. One is the bronze Mercury in the Bargello, balanced on one foot on a zephyr's head as if springing into air. The other is the marble Rape of the Sabines in the Loggia de Lanzi, made for Francesco de' Medici and named only after it was done. The entry also lists his great fountain at Bologna, his Boboli garden fountains, and a bronze horse statue of Cosimo de' Medici.
britannica-1911-breda:
Breda is a fortified town in the Dutch province of North Brabant, set where the canalised rivers Merk and Aa meet, 15 miles east-north-east of Roozendaal. Its population in 1900 was 26,296. Old defences were partly taken down, yet lines of works and low ground that can be flooded still guard the town.

Sights picked out include the town hall, a fine quay and a park, plus several churches. The main Protestant church is Gothic, begun late in the 13th century, with a choir from 1410 and the grand tomb of Count Engelbert II of Nassau. Since 1828 the town has held a royal military academy, and its round domed prison, with 208 cells in four tiers, gets a full account.
britannica-1911-brunhilda:
Brunhilda, or Brunechildis (died 613), was a queen of Austrasia and daughter of Athanagild, king of the Visigoths. In 567 Sigebert, reigning at Metz, asked for her in marriage. She then abjured Arianism, converted to the orthodox faith, and the wedding was celebrated at Metz, with the poet Fortunatus, then at the Frankish court, composing the marriage song.

Jealousy lit the feud that fills her story. Chilperic, Sigebert's brother and king of the west Franks, hastened to marry her sister Galswintha, then, at his mistress Fredegond's instigation, had his wife assassinated. Sigebert sought vengeance but accepted compensation brokered by Guntram: the cities of Bordeaux, Cahors and Limoges, with Bearn and Bigorre. The treaty did not stop war breaking out again. While her husband lived Brunhilda played a secondary part.
britannica-1911-caravaggio-michelangelo-:
Michelangelo Amerighi da Caravaggio (1569–1609) was an Italian painter. He took his name from his birth village in Lombardy. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his fierce, brief life. He began as a mason's labourer in his youth. His powerful genius drove him to painting instead. He worked at it with unstoppable energy and force. He despised every kind of idealism in art.

Caravaggio led the Naturalisti, painters who copied nature without softening it. His style used bold contrasts of light and shadow. A fierce temper ran through his whole career. In a gambling quarrel at Rome he killed a man. He fled to Naples and then to Malta. Prison there, and a wounding in Sicily, followed. Pardoned, he set out back toward Rome in 1609. He was arrested by mistake on the way. He died of fever on a beach that year. The entry names his Entombment as among his best works.
britannica-1911-caravaggio-polidoro-cald:
Polidoro Caldara da Caravaggio (1495 or 1492–1543) was an Italian painter. He was celebrated for frieze and other decoration work. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his rise from poverty. He began as a mere mortar-carrier in the Vatican. There he carried mortar for the artists at work. His talent caught the eye of Raphael himself. Raphael was then painting his great works in the Loggie.

Most of Polidoro's works have since perished. They survive in the fine etchings of Bartoli and Alberti. His master was Maturino of Florence, whose works shared the same fate. When Rome was sacked in 1527, Polidoro fled to Naples. He went on to Messina and found much work there. He gained a considerable fortune in Sicily. He was about to return to the Italian mainland. An assistant, Tonno Calabrese, robbed and murdered him in 1543. The entry names a Crucifixion at Messina among his chief paintings.
britannica-1911-carpi-girolamo-da:
Girolamo da Carpi (1501–1556) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian historical and portrait painter born at Ferrara.
