He was one of the best pupils of Benvenuto Garofalo. A strong draw toward Correggio's work led him to leave Ferrara and spend years copying that master's paintings at Parma, Modena, and elsewhere.

He learned Correggio's manner so well that he could pass off his own pictures as originals by the master. The entry suggests that some works still credited to Correggio are really his. His best paintings include a Descent of the Holy Spirit at Rovigo, a Madonna and an Adoration of the Magi at Bologna, and a St George and a St Jerome at Ferrara. The short account mixes real skill with a sharp warning about false attribution.
britannica-1911-carpi-ugo-da:
Ugo da Carpi is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian painter of the fifteenth century who was long held to have invented printing in chiaroscuro. Later research by Michael Huber and Johann Gottlob Immanuel Breitkopf showed the art was already practised in Germany. Johann Ulrich Pilgrim and Nikolaus Alexander Mair used it at least as early as 1499, while Da Carpi's oldest print dates from 1518.

The entry explains the method he used. Chiaroscuro printing works from several blocks, and Da Carpi generally used three: one for the outline and dark shadows, one for the lighter shadows, and one for the half-tint. With them he printed engravings after several pictures and after some of Raphael's cartoons. A Sybil, a Descent from the Cross, and a History of Simon the Sorcerer are named as his most remarkable prints. Credit for the invention moves elsewhere, but his craft keeps its place.
britannica-1911-chaetosomatida:
Chaetosomatida, a small group of tiny free living water creatures, are described in a 1911 Britannica article. They are most often placed as a side group of the round worms. One scholar calls them creeping round worms. They are found most often among seaweed in mild seas, and some live in fresh water.

Two genera have swollen heads, and a third has none that stands out. The mouth sits at the front end, ringed by spikes or hooks. Scattered hairs cover the body. Near the rear, rows of stout pegs let the beasts creep along. Females run a bit larger than males, at near one and a half millimeters long in one kind. The gut runs from mouth to a vent near the hind end.
britannica-1911-chanda:
Chanda is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town and district of British India. The town lies in the Nagpur division of the Central Provinces. A count from 1901 gives the town 17,803 people. It stands where the Virai and Jharpat rivers meet. It was once the capital of the Gond kingdom of Chanda. That kingdom rose on the ruins of a Hindu state. It lasted until 1751, the text notes.

A stone wall still rings the town in a long circuit. Old temples and tombs stand within and near it. The district at large is rich in old remains. Local work turns out cotton, silk, and brass ware. Leather slippers are also made and sold. Hills dot most of the district land. In the east they rise to a broad high tableland. The Wainganga river flows through the region.
britannica-1911-cicada:
Cicada (Cicadidae) are insects of the homopterous division of the Hemiptera, generally of large size, with toothed front legs and two pairs of large clear wings. Males are remarkable for their shrill song, heard a quarter of a mile away or more. A pair of vocal organs in the thorax, each a stretched drum driven by a strong muscle, makes that sound. The song is believed to serve as a sexual call to the females.

Long life sets cicadas apart, surpassing that of all other insects. One North American species is said to take seventeen years to mature. Females lay eggs in tree branches with a saw-like ovipositor, and the young fall, burrow and feed for years on roots below ground. Pupae then climb a plant stem and free the perfect insect. Only one species is found in England, in the southern counties.
britannica-1911-cigoli-lodovico-cardi-da:
Cigoli, Lodovico Cardi da (1559–1613) was an Italian painter, architect and poet, born at Cigoli in Tuscany. He learned under Alessandro Allori and Santi di Tito, then formed his own style at Florence from Michelangelo, Correggio, Andrea del Sarto and Pontormo. Correggio shaped him most of all those masters. Attacks by enemies and intense work on a wax anatomical model brought on three years of alienation of mind.

After Lombardy he returned to Florence and won a prize with an Ecce Homo painted against Passignani and Caravaggio. A Martyrdom of Stephen earned him the name of the Florentine Correggio, and major works stand at Rome, the Villa Borghese and Florence. He was a good, solid draughtsman with a rich, harmonious palette. Death came, it is said, from grief at the failure of his last fresco in Santa Maria Maggiore.
britannica-1911-cocanada:
Cocanada, or Coconada, is a town of British India in the Godavari district of Madras, on the coast at the extreme north of the Godavari delta, about 315 miles north of Madras. Its people numbered 48,096 in 1901, showing an increase of 18 per cent in the decade. It is the administrative headquarters of the district and the chief port on the Coromandel coast after Madras. Navigable channels link it with the canal system of the Godavari delta.

Shipping trade has declined through the silting of the anchorage and the construction of the railway, the entry says. The anchorage is an open roadstead with two lighthouses, and a branch line joins the town to Samalkot on the East Coast railway. Chief exports are rice, cotton, sugar and oilseeds, with mills established for cleaning rice. A second-grade college, a high school and a literary association serve the town's education and letters.
britannica-1911-coda: Coda is a short music entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the closing passage of music. The word is Italian for tail, from the Latin cauda. A coda brings a movement, or a whole work, to its end. The form grew from the plain chords of a cadence into a fuller, free-standing shape. In a set of variations, the coda stands apart from the endings of the single parts and ties the whole work off. The article credits Beethoven with raising the coda to high weight.
britannica-1911-collingwood-canada:
Collingwood is a town of Simcoe county, Ontario, in Canada, 90 miles north-west of Toronto. It stands on Georgian Bay and on the Grand Trunk railway. Its people numbered 5,755 in 1901. The town forms the east end point of two steamer lines. Those lines serve ports on Lakes Huron and Superior.

Work and trade give the town its weight. A large stone dry-dock and shipyard serve the lake fleet. A pork factory and saw and planing mills add to its plant. Steel works stand beside the shipbuilding yard. Exports run chiefly to lumber, grain and farm produce. The entry is short and plain in scope. It fixes the town's place, its lake links and its main lines of work. No history of its founding is given.
britannica-1911-cruz-e-silva-antonio-din:
Antonio Diniz da Cruz e Silva (1731–1799) was a Portuguese heroic-comic poet, son of a Lisbon carpenter who left for Brazil before the poet's birth. His mother raised and schooled the family by needlework. Diniz studied with the Oratorians, took a law degree at Coimbra in 1753, and gave six years to letters in Lisbon. In 1756 he helped found the Arcadia Lusitana and drew up its statutes.

Service as a magistrate took Diniz to Castello de Vide and then to Elvas, where he spent ten years. At Elvas he watched a garrison town split between bishop and governor, and hoarded its odd characters in memory. A quarrel of 1768 over holy water at a cathedral door gave him his plot. From it he built his masterpiece, Hyssope, a satire on the vanities he had seen. His poems appeared in six volumes after his death, and Hyssope kept his fame.
britannica-1911-dalriada:
Dalriada is the name of two ancient Gaelic kingdoms, one in Ireland and one in Scotland, and this short 1911 Britannica entry explains the link. The name means the home of the descendants of Riada. Irish Dalriada was the district that now forms the northern part of county Antrim. About the year 500 some of its people crossed the sea to Scotland.

There they founded a second Dalriada in Argyllshire. For a time the Scottish kingdom stayed under the Irish one. About 575 King Aidan won its freedom. One of Aidan's heirs, Kenneth, became king of the Picts about 843. After that the name Dalriada slowly fell out of use in both lands. The entry points to Skene's Celtic Scotland for more.
britannica-1911-feltre-morto-da:
Feltre, Morto da is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Italian painter of the Venetian school. He worked at the close of the fifteenth century and the start of the sixteenth. Whether the name Morto, meaning dead, came from his gloomy temper is disputed. He probably studied first in Venice, then went early to Rome.

The article traces his part in a famous style of ornament. In Rome and at Pozzuoli he studied the painted decoration of ancient underground chambers, the grotte. From them he formed a fanciful arabesque manner that took the name grottesche, the source of the English word grotesque. It follows him to Florence, to work beside Giorgione in Venice, and home to Feltre.
britannica-1911-filicaja-vincenzo-da:
Italian poet Vincenzo da Filicaja, born in Florence in sixteen forty two, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He sprang from an ancient and noble family of that city. A note in one of his letters shows his parents were in easy circumstances. He had all the gains of a broad schooling.

He studied first under the Jesuits of Florence, then at the university of Pisa. At Pisa his mind was stored with learning in many branches of letters. It also took in the past glory of the Pisan republic. He noted the order of Saint Stephen, whose naval men guarded Tuscan trade from corsairs. After five years at Pisa he returned to Florence. There he wed a senator's daughter and withdrew to a small villa nearby.
britannica-1911-fiorenzuola-d-arda: Fiorenzuola d Arda is a town in Emilia in Italy, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Piacenza, south east of that city by rail. About seven thousand eight hundred people lived there in 1901. The town has a fine square with an old tower at its centre. Near it lies a Cistercian abbey with a Gothic church and a large brick cloister.
britannica-1911-fonsagrada:
Fonsagrada is a town of north-western Spain, in the province of Lugo, 25 miles east-north-east of Lugo by road. Its population in 1900 was 17,302. It stands 3,166 feet above the sea, on the watershed between the rivers Rodil and Suarna. It is an important market for all kinds of farm produce, and it manufactures linen and frieze, a coarse woollen cloth. Its high place among the hills shapes both its trade and its limits, the entry shows.

Trade at Fonsagrada stays mainly local. The mountainous character of the country round it, and the lack of a railway or navigable river, bar any large export trade from growing. The short entry thus gives a mountain market town measured by its height, its rivers, its market and its cloth. The hosted file opens with the closing pages of the article on Fondi, an Italian town, before reaching Fonsagrada itself.
britannica-1911-fonseca-manoel-deodoro-d:
Manoel Deodoro da Fonseca (1827-1892) was the first president of the United States of Brazil. He was born at Alagoas on 5 August 1827, third son of a lieutenant-colonel. Educated at the military school of Rio de Janeiro, he had reached captain when war broke out in 1864 against Montevideo and then against Solano Lopez, dictator of Paraguay. His courage won distinction, and by the war's end in 1870 he was a colonel, later a general of division.

Fonseca held several military commands, then in 1886 became governor of Rio Grande do Sul. There he threw himself into politics, took up the republican opinions then spreading, and sheltered republican speakers with his authority. The government removed him at the close of that year and recalled him to the capital. The entry follows him from disgrace to the revolution that made him head of the republic, and through his stormy presidency to his fall.
britannica-1911-franklin-canada:
Franklin was an organised district of Canada stretching from the Arctic Circle to the North Pole. It was formed by order-in-council on 2 October 1895 and took in many islands and peninsulas, among them Banks, Victoria, Melville, Bathurst, Prince of Wales, and Baffin Land. Of these, Baffin Land alone reaches south of the Arctic Circle.

The area was put at about 500,000 square miles, yet the people numbered only a few Indians, Eskimo, and fur traders. Musk-oxen, polar bears, foxes, and other fur-bearing animals were found in large numbers. The district took its name from Sir John Franklin, the Arctic explorer, and the entry is a brief gazetteer note on its bounds and contents.
britannica-1911-friedrichroda: Friedrichroda is a summer resort in the duchy of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, Germany, at the north foot of the Thuringian Forest, 13 miles by rail south-west of Gotha. About 4500 people live there among fir-clad hills. The town has many handsome villa residences, a Kurhaus, and a sanatorium. Close by stands Reinhardsbrunn, the ducal hunting seat built from the ruins of the noted Benedictine monastery founded in 1085. The entry is a short resort note.
britannica-1911-fulda:
Fulda is a town and episcopal see of Germany in Hesse-Nassau, between the Rhön and Vogel hills, 69 miles north-east of Frankfort. Its cathedral, built early in the 18th century on the model of St Peter at Rome, keeps an ancient crypt holding the bones of St Boniface. The round Michaelskirche of 822 stands by the former monastery. The library holds over 80,000 printed books.

The town exists because of its abbey, founded in 744 by Sturm, pupil of Boniface, as a centre of mission work. Its school, where Alcuin, Hrabanus Maurus, and Walafrid Strabo taught, led the learning of the early middle ages. The abbot became a bishop in 1752 and Fulda a prince-bishopric, secularised in 1802. The town passed to Prussia in 1866, and a new bishopric was founded in 1829. Weaving, dyeing, and brewing lead its modern trades.
britannica-1911-gama-vasco-da:
Vasco da Gama was born about 1460 and died in 1524, a Portuguese navigator. The 1911 Britannica life hails him as finder of the sea route to India. He was born at Sines, a small seaport in Alemtejo. Little is known of his early years or of his youth. His line came of a noble house noted as far back as 1166.

That line can be traced without gaps only from the year 1280. His father Estevao was civil governor of Sines in his day. Vasco was the third son of that governor of the port. The year of his birth was the year Prince Henry the Navigator died. All Portugal's sea fame traces back to that prince's foresight.
britannica-1911-gastropoda:
Gastropoda, in the 1911 Britannica, is a very long zoology article on the second of the five classes of molluscs. Snails, slugs and their kin make up the class. The article's core idea is torsion: as the animal develops, its visceral sac twists, so the body loses the plain symmetry of other molluscs.

The opening works through that twisting in detail, using the growth of Trochus as the worked example, with figures. From there the article covers the shell, the mantle cavity and the organs, group by group. Its classification divides the class into the Streptoneura and the Euthyneura, the latter holding forms such as the Pulmonata, the land and freshwater snails and slugs. Readers get both a full anatomy and a scheme for sorting the many families of the class.
britannica-1911-gelada:
Gelada is the Abyssinian name of a large species of baboon, covered in this 1911 Britannica article. It differs from the members of the genus Papio in that its nostrils sit some distance above the end of the muzzle. For that trait it has been made the type of a genus of its own, under the name Theropithecus gelada.

The old males wear a heavy mantle of long brown hair over the forequarters, save for the bare chest, which is reddish flesh colour. In that mantle the gelada recalls the Arabian baboon, and some have proposed putting the two species in one genus. The gelada lives in the mountains of Abyssinia, where, like other baboons, it comes down in droves to plunder farmed lands. A second species or race, darker in hair, lives on the eastern borders of Abyssinia.
britannica-1911-gnathopoda: Gnathopoda is a term used in zoology as a proposed new name for the group called Arthropoda. The word means jaw-footed. It points to a trait of the group: some of the side limbs near the mouth work as jaws. Those limbs are feet in form, but they serve the mouth in use. The name thus rests on one clear mark of the animals it covers, rather than on their shape as a whole.
britannica-1911-grenada:
Grenada is the southernmost of the Windward Islands, in the British West Indies, lying 140 miles south-west of Barbados and 85 miles north of Trinidad. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its shape as oval: 21 miles long, 12 broad at most, with an area of 133 square miles. A well-wooded mountain range runs its length from north to south.

Mount Catharine, at 2,750 feet, is the highest point. The island is volcanic, and its chief natural curiosity is the Grand Etang, a circular lake of 13 acres in an old crater, 1,740 feet above the sea. A larger crater lake, Lake Antoine, lies in the north-east. The entry notes sulphur and fuller's earth among the worked minerals, and fruit growing and cattle raising on the low ground. From geography the article moves to the island's history, government and spice trade.
britannica-1911-griselda:
Griselda is a heroine of romance, said to have been the wife of Walter, marquis of Saluzzo, in the 11th century. Her sufferings were treated as history by Boccaccio and Petrarch, though Boccaccio most likely took the tale from a Provençal fabliau. He placed it among the stories of the tenth day of the Decameron, written about 1350.

Petrarch retold the story in a Latin letter of 1373, and his version shaped most later treatments. It was printed about 1470, translated into French in 1484, and dramatised as early as 1395. Chaucer followed Petrarch in the Canterbury Tales, and Dekker, Chettle and Haughton staged the story in 1603. Ballads and a 1619 chap-book, The History of Patient Grisel, carried her patience to a wide readership.
britannica-1911-guarda:
Guarda is an episcopal city in Portugal. It is capital of an administrative district of the same name. It once lay in the province of Beira. Two railway lines serve it. Its population in 1900 was 6,124. The city stands 3,370 feet above sea-level. It sits at the north-eastern end of the Serra da Estrella. It overlooks the fertile valley of the river Côa.

Ancient walls surround the city. It holds a ruined castle and a fine 16th-century cathedral. A sanatorium for consumptives is also noted. Its trades cover coarse cloth, grain, wine and live stock. Sancho I founded Guarda in 1199. The site was the Roman Lencia Oppidana. He meant it, as its name says, to guard against Moorish invasion. The wider district held 261,630 people in 1900.
britannica-1911-haida: Haida are a North American native people of Skittagetan stock, noted in a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. They still live in their first home, the Queen Charlotte islands in British Columbia. They are skilled seamen who make long fishing trips in cedar wood canoes. Their carving and basket work are also praised. In past times they raided coast tribes, and slavery passed by birth, the slaves being war captives. Their count, some seven thousand in the mid last century, had fallen to a few hundred.
britannica-1911-hill-octavia-and-miranda:
Octavia Hill (1838– ) and Miranda Hill (1836–1910) were English philanthropic workers, born in London, granddaughters of Dr Southwood Smith, the sanitary reformer. Octavia saw early how bad London housing bred lethargy in the poor. Ruskin backed her plan to free a few families from such surroundings and supplied the starting money.

For £750 she bought the lease of three houses in a poor Marylebone court, repaired them, and let them in two-room sets. Within eighteen months the scheme paid 5% interest and all its costs. She collected the rents herself, meeting the tenants and enforcing self-respecting habits. More houses followed, eleven more in 1869 alone, and friends placed whole groups under her care.
britannica-1911-honda:
Honda is a town on the Magdalena river, set about 650 ft. above sea-level where the little Guali stream enters the great river. The surviving text opens mid-article, with the town's population put at 7,000. Honda overlooks the rapids of the Magdalena and is shut in by spurs of the Eastern and Central Cordilleras. Its climate is hot and damp.

The town dates from the start of the 17th century and has been a traffic centre for three hundred years. An iron bridge crosses the Guali, and a suspension bridge spans the Magdalena at the rapids' head. A railway of 18 m. runs to La Dorada, where the lower river steamers unload. Until 1908 most traffic for Bogotá crossed here and went 67 m. by mule over the rough camino real. It now passes to smaller steamboats for Girardot, and thence by rail. An earthquake nearly destroyed Honda in 1808.
britannica-1911-howel-dda:
Howel Dda, the Good (d. 950), was prince of Deheubarth in south central Wales from before 915, and king of Wales from 943 to 950. He was a grandson of Rhodri Mawr, who had united nearly the whole of Wales. Howel succeeded Rhodri's younger son Cadell in Deheubarth, married Elen, daughter of the last king of Dyfed, and added Kidweli and Gwyr to his lands. When Idwal of Gwynedd fell to the English in 943, he took Gwynedd too.

Both princes had done homage to the English kings, Edward the Elder and Aethelstan, in 922 and 926. Howel attended the witans of the English kingdom and witnessed some ten charters between 931 and 949, safe from attack on his eastern side. His lasting fame is as a lawgiver. The Welsh laws in their Venedotian, Demetian and Gwentian forms are tied to his name, and are said to have been written down by Bleggwryd, archdeacon of Llandaff.
britannica-1911-hyposulphite-of-soda: Hyposulphite of Soda is a short chemistry entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It gives the name first used for the substance known in chemistry as sodium thiosulphate. The older name still held common use at the time. Photographers above all kept it, since they used the chemical as a fixer. In strict naming, sodium hyposulphite is a different salt, of hyposulphurous acid. The entry points to the article on sulphur for the rest.
britannica-1911-igualada:
Igualada is a town of north east Spain in the province of Barcelona. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the left bank of the river Noya. That stream feeds the Llobregat, and a rail line ends at the town. Its count in 1900 was 10,442 souls in the town. It serves as the chief market of a rich farm district.

Wine grapes grow well in that district, the entry notes with care. An old town of tight, bent streets forms the core of Igualada. Ruins of a fort and of old ramparts still show there in part. A new town of broad streets and fine houses spreads beside it. Work since 1880 spans cloth, linen, wool, soap, and leather goods.
britannica-1911-loanda:
Loanda, also called São Paulo de Loanda, is a seaport of West Africa described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the Portuguese province of Angola. The town sits on a bay between the rivers Bango and Kwanza. A long narrow island of sand shields the bay from the surf.

A low sandy cliff backs the shore and ends in a bold point crowned by Fort San Miguel. Water at the bay mouth runs twenty fathoms deep or more. The bay has silted up a good deal over time. Still, good anchorage lies about a mile and a half off shore in seven to fourteen fathoms. Ships unload into lighters and are seldom held up by weather. Grand buildings, the offices of rule and the bishop palace among them, stand on higher ground.
britannica-1911-meleda:
Meleda, an island in the Adriatic Sea, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. Its Serbo-Croatian name is Mljet. It is the most southerly and easterly of the larger Adriatic islands of Dalmatia. Its people numbered 1,617 in 1900. It lies south of the Sabioncello promontory, across the Meleda Channel.

The island is twenty-three miles long. Its average breadth is two miles. It is of volcanic origin. Numerous chasms and gorges cut it. The longest gorge, the Babinopolje, joins the north and south of the island. Port Palazzo, the chief harbour, lies on the north. Tourist steamers call there. Meleda has been held to be the Melita of a famous shipwreck. On that island, tradition says, Saint Paul was cast ashore. That view was first set out in the tenth century, by Constantine Porphyrogenitus. As at Malta, a Saint Paul's Bay is still shown there.
britannica-1911-myriapoda:
Many-legged beasts lose their old class in a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Myriapoda was the name for centipedes and millipedes as one group. Linnaeus had lumped them with shell beasts and spiders as wingless kinds. Latreille set them apart under that Greek name in 1796. Savigny then split them from insects by their mouth parts.

Leach fixed the group in 1814 with two clear halves. Latreille later urged that the two halves stood far apart. Millipedes, he held, stood near the shell beasts in true kin. Centipedes stood near spiders and insects by his reading then. That split view has won, the entry plainly tells us. The two sorts now rank as two classes of their own.
britannica-1911-nagykikinda: Nagykikinda, a town of Hungary in the county of Torontál, is given a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands one hundred and fifty-two miles south-east of Budapest by rail. The census of 1900 counted 24,843 people there. About sixty in every hundred of them were Serbians. The town is one of the centres of the famed wheat country of the Banat. Its flour milling industry is therefore important to the district. Fruit farming and cattle rearing are also carried on widely in the land around it.
britannica-1911-nerbudda:
Nerbudda, also spelled Narbada, is a river of India, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows its course. It is held to mark the line between Hindustan proper and the Deccan. It rises on Amarkantak hill in Rewa state and winds for its first two hundred miles among the Mandla hills. At Jubbulpore it passes through the Marble Rocks and enters its valley between two ranges. Then it runs west to the Gulf of Cambay.

Its full course runs to about eight hundred miles, ending in a broad estuary below Broach. The river is not used for watering crops, and boats work only its lower stretch. In holiness it ranks second only to the Ganges. The greatest act for a pilgrim is to walk from the sea to the source and back on the far bank. That trip takes one to two years.
britannica-1911-novelda: Novelda is a town in the east of Spain, in the province of Alicante. The short 1911 Britannica note sets it on the right bank of the river Vinalopo. A rail line from Madrid to Alicante runs through the town. Its count in 1900 was 11,388 people. Flat, rich farms round it yield wine, dates, oranges, oil, saffron, and aniseed. Work in town spans tanneries and the making of soap and chocolate, while the women make fine lace.
britannica-1911-ouida:
Ouida was the pen name of Maria Louise Ramee, an English novelist born at Bury Saint Edmunds in 1839. The 1911 Britannica entry says the name came from a child attempt to say Louisa. Her father was French and her mother English, and London became her home young. Magazine tales in the New Monthly and Bentley journals started her career.

Her first story came out in 1860 and was reissued as Held in Bondage in 1863. Strathmore, Chandos, and Under Two Flags followed in quick order to wide sales. Moths in 1880 joined them as among her best and most typical works. Stories for children, Bimbi in 1882, show her in a gentler vein.
britannica-1911-pagoda:
Pagoda is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Eastern word for a temple. The word came through Portuguese traders in India in the 1500s. Behind it may stand a Persian term for a house of an idol, or a Sanskrit word for what is holy.

The article gives the main senses one by one. A pagoda is a temple of steep, tapering shape in India and the Far East. In lands of the Buddhist faith it can mean a tower of many sides that holds holy relics. Loose use stretches the word to any place of worship that is not of the Christian or Muslim faith. The name also marked a gold coin of south India. That coin sense gave rise to a phrase about the wealth of the Indies.
britannica-1911-palestrina-giovanni-pier:
Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, the great church composer, fills a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in 1526 at Palestrina, foot of the Sabine hills. His name shows in a swarm of forms in old records. He spent time at Rome in his youth and learned his craft there. In 1547 he wed Lucrezia de Goris and raised a family.

Pope Julius the Third raised him to head the Julian Chapel in 1551. His pay was six scudi a month, with a house to live in. His first book of Masses came out three years later. In 1555 the pope put him among the Sistine Chapel singers. That post drew a fight, for he was a wedded man.
britannica-1911-penda:
Penda, king of Mercia, who died in 654 or 655, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Pybba. He may have taken the throne in 626, though his firm kingship dates from 633. In that year he and the Welsh king overthrew Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield Chase.

The article follows a reign of near constant war. Penda slew King Oswald in 642 and raided Northumbria again and again. He drove Cenwalh of Wessex from his throne for casting off his sister. In 654 he attacked the East Angles and killed their king, Anna. The next year he invaded Northumbria despite bribes meant to turn him back. There he was beaten and slain by the river Winwaed. Though a pagan himself, he let Christian teaching enter Middle Anglia under his son Peada.
britannica-1911-rehan-ada:
Ada Rehan (1860– ) was an American actress, born Ada Crehan in Limerick, Ireland, on the 22nd of April 1860. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces her path from a first small part at Newark in 1874 through years of stock company work. In 1879 she joined Augustin Daly's company, and his training brought out her gift.

Under Daly she shone first in modern comedy, then in the older plays. Her great parts were Peggy in The Country Girl, Julia in The Hunchback, and above all Katharina in The Taming of the Shrew. She also played Rosalind and Viola, and toured with the company to England, France, and Germany. Her life-size portrait as Katharina hangs in the Shakespeare Memorial gallery at Stratford-on-Avon.
britannica-1911-rhondda:
Rhondda, once called Ystradyfodwg, is an urban district and parliamentary division of Glamorganshire in South Wales, and this 1911 Britannica entry maps it. The district runs twelve miles long and about four and three-quarter miles across at its widest. It is made of two main valleys, named for their rivers: the Rhondda Fawr, the greater, and the Rhondda Fach, the lesser. They meet at Porth, and the joined valley runs on toward Pontypridd.

The valleys are narrow and winding, walled by steep hills. Heights rise from about 560 feet near Trehafod to 1,950 feet at Carn Moesen at the head of the main valley. A steep ridge, Cefn-rhondda, parts the two valleys. Smaller side valleys include Cwmparc, Clydach Vale, and Cymmer. The entry gives the district's acreage and then turns to its towns, mines, and people.
britannica-1911-ronda:
Ronda is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in southern Spain, in the province of Malaga. It stands on the river Guadiaro, with 20,995 people in 1900. The town is built on a high rock, nearly ringed by the river. The Guadiaro runs through a sheer chasm 530 feet deep.

That chasm splits the old town from the new. Three bridges cross it: one said to be Roman, one Moorish, and a newer one from 1761 that spans the stream in a single arch at a height near 255 feet. The old town keeps a Moorish air, with narrow, steep, crooked lanes and old towers. The bull-ring at Ronda is one of the finest in Spain and holds ten thousand people.
britannica-1911-silva-antonio-jose-da:
Antonio Jose da Silva was a writer of plays in Portugal who lived from seventeen five to seventeen thirty-nine. He was born at Rio de Janeiro and came to the old land at age eight. His folk were Jews who had fled the harsh church court to Brazil. That court then chased them there as well.

His mother was seized and put through pain, and the kin moved to Lisbon. He read law and joined his father at the bar. His first play came in seventeen thirty-three. Five years on he and his wife were seized on a charge of secret faith. That charge sealed his fate.
britannica-1911-sindhi-and-lahnda:
Sindhi and Lahnda are two linked tongues of the north west of India. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places them in the outer band of Indo Aryan speech. Sindhi is the language of Sindh, while Lahnda means the western tongue. In 1901 each was spoken by well over three million people.

Both tongues sat apart from the main Midland spread for ages. That isolation let them grow in shared and distinct ways at once. Sindhi comes straight from a named old Prakrit form, the entry says. A key dialect of Sindhi in Cutch shows mixing with Gujarati. Persian loan words enter both through Muslim rule in the region.
britannica-1911-taurida:
Taurida, a province of south Russia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It takes in the peninsula of Crimea and a tract of mainland to its north. The Black Sea and the Sea of Azov wash its south shores. In 1906 its folk were reckoned at over one million six hundred thousand.

The mainland part is a flat steppe of black earth with no forests. Grain is its wealth, and most land fit for the plough is sown. Rye, wheat, oats, and barley lead the crops, with wide vineyards in Crimea. Salt is the one mineral raised, from ponds at the mouth of the Dnieper. Grain, salt, fish, wool, and tallow sail out from ports on both seas. Stock breeding is also a great line of work.
britannica-1911-towanda:
Towanda, a borough in Pennsylvania, is sketched in a short place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It is the county seat of Bradford county, on the west bank of the Susquehanna river. The town stands about 730 feet above the sea, ringed by high hills, some 50 miles north-west of Wilkes-Barré. Its counts ran 4,169 in 1890, 4,663 in 1900, and 4,281 in 1910. Two railways serve it, the Lehigh Valley and the Susquehanna and New York.

The borough holds the museum of the Bradford County Historical Society, and its land is given to farming and stock raising. The first settlement was made in 1786. The village was laid out in 1812, became county seat that year, and was incorporated as Towanda in 1828. Its name is an Indian word said to mean where we bury the dead.
candida:
Bernard Shaw's play Candida, dated 1898 on its title page, opens on an October morning in London's north-east suburbs. The Reverend James Morell, a popular Christian socialist clergyman, keeps a happy parsonage with his wife Candida. Into the house comes Eugene Marchbanks, a shy young poet who loves her hopelessly and says so. Shaw sets the triangle among typewriters, sermons, and parish callers.

Inside, Candida nurses both men through the crisis her husband's confidence cannot see. Marchbanks offers poetry and worship; Morell offers the strength Candida herself has built and sheltered. Her choice, explained in one of Shaw's famous auction speeches, turns the Victorian angel of the house into the manager of it. Readers get an early, humane Shaw: a domestic comedy whose love scene is an argument, and whose heroine wins by understanding both men better than they understand themselves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achrida:
Achrida is a titular see in Upper Albania, once medieval Bulgaria's metropolis and capital, now the little Ochrida village on its lake, ancient Lacus Lychnitis. In antiquity the city was Lychnidus, a frontier outpost in Illyrian wars with Rome and later a point on the great Via Egnatia highway. Its first known bishop was Zosimus, about 344.

In the sixth century an earthquake destroyed it, but Justinian, born nearby, rebuilt it and made it capital of the prefecture of Illyria and ecclesiastical capital of the southern Danubian empire. Duchesne disputes the claim that it was Justiniana Prima, giving that honour to Scupi. At its height Achrida counted ten metropolitan and six episcopal dioceses subject to it, until its patriarchate was abolished in 1767 by Sultan Mustapha.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-fulda:
Adam of Fulda, born about 1450 and dead after 1537, was among his age's most learned musicians, a monk of Franconia, taking his name from that country's capital city. At the time, contrapuntal music flourished above all in the Netherlands, Josquin its brilliant star. Adam, a disciple of the Dutch teachers himself, ultimately became their rival.

His fame rests on a famous music treatise written in 1490 and printed by Gerbert in his Scriptores ecclesiastici de musica sacra. The treatise runs to forty-five chapters, treating the invention and praise of music, voice, sound, tone, keys, measured and figured music, tone relations, intervals, and consonances. A list of his compositions appears in the Quellen-Lexikon. Calling himself musicus ducalis, he probably served some prince, possibly the Bishop of Wurzburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alabanda: Alabanda, Caria's titular see in Asia Minor, is thought to be today's Arab-Hissar, a present-day identification. Its bishops are listed from 451 to 879, a span of over four centuries. Anciently its people were famed for luxurious habits. A district court sat there in imperial times, and the town flourished greatly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-andrad:
Alonso Andrada was a biographer and ascetic writer, born at Toledo in Spain in 1590 and dead at Madrid in June 1672. Before entering the Society of Jesus in 1612 he read philosophy at Toledo, and afterwards was rector of Plasencia and minister in foreign countries. His later years produced about thirty-four volumes across varied subjects, some notable for learning, sound doctrine, and pleasing style. These partly hide a careless, over-simple streak.

He is chiefly known as the continuator of Nieremberg's Varones Ilustres, biographies of distinguished members of the Society of Jesus. His Guide to Virtue and Imitation of Our Lady deserves special mention. The entry presents a prolific Jesuit author whose vast output, uneven in care, still holds works of real learning and doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-de-oje:
Alonso de Ojeda was an explorer, born at Cuenca about 1466 and dead on Santo Domingo about 1508. Of impoverished noble family, he began in service to the Dukes of Medina Sidonia. Fonseca of Burgos, later Patriarch of the Indies, soon became his patron. Fonseca got Ojeda onto Columbus's second voyage to the New World. There his daring in battle distinguished him, though he was unduly harsh to the natives.

Back at Hispaniola with his former associate Cosa, Ojeda conceived mainland colonies between Cabo de Vela and the Gulf of Urabá. After petitioning the government, he sailed; disaster struck, and all but Ojeda and one other perished. The two escaped to shore, succoured by those left with the ships. Undespairing, he founded San Sebastián, leaving Pizarro in charge while sailing to Hispaniola for supplies. Shipwrecked, he reached Santo Domingo after privations and died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amida:
Amida, or Diarbekir, is an Armenian Rite diocese in Mesopotamia, Asiatic Turkey. Its city's foundation was wrongly attributed to Tigranes I or Tigranes the Great of Armenia, and the city is named as Tigranocerte or Dikranagherd. Greeks and Romans called it Amida, Turks Kara-Amid, Amid the Black, but its usual Arabic name is Diarbekir.

Diarbekir holds an Armenian Catholic bishop, a Syrian Catholic bishop, a Syrian Jacobite bishop, a Chaldean Catholic archbishop, and a Greek Orthodox prelate under Antioch's patriarch. Its Latin Mission dates from Père Jean-Baptiste de Saint Aignan in 1667.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amphilochius-:
Bishop of Sida in Pamphylia during the first half of the fifth century, Amphilochius sat at the Council of Ephesus in 431. There he opposed the Messalians and signed the condemnation and deposition of Nestorius. He proved less firm later, showing sympathy for Dioscorus of Alexandria at Chalcedon. He consented only with reluctance to his condemnation.

Though he signed the tome of Pope Leo and the canons of Chalcedon, he wrote to Emperor Leo in 458 denying the authority of that council. Later evidence, quoted by Photius from Eulogius of Alexandria, points to his eventual acceptance and subscription. Only one brief letter fragment from him survives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-de-an:
Portuguese Jesuit Antonio de Andrada, born at Oleiros in 1580 and dead at Goa in 1634, is remembered as the pioneer missionary and explorer of Tibet in the seventeenth century. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1596 and served as chief missionary in the Indies from 1600 to 1624. After great hardship he reached Tibet in 1624, was kindly received by its head ruler, and returned to Agra for fellow workers before founding a mission centre at Chaparangue.

Recalled to Goa as superior of the Indies, he died in Goa, and the article reports that he was poisoned for the faith. His letters to superiors gave a vivid and faithful account of his discoveries and labours. They were later published in Spanish and French and gathered into a 1629 history of events in the kingdom of Tibet. The entry is a compact tale of travel, mission, and report writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attuda: Attuda was a titular see, a former bishopric kept on the books in name, in Phrygia in Asia Minor. The whole entry is a single line of reference. It points readers to the list of its bishops, covering the years 431 to 879, as printed in Gams on page 446. No bishop, event, or local history is described beyond that pointer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benda:
Benda is a brief entry on a titular see, or honorary bishopric, in Albania, in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its story is tied to the neighbouring sees of Narenta and Mostar, whose bishops shifted titles and homes across centuries of border change. A bishop at the council of 879 already carries a title linked to this line.

By the middle of the 1300s Narenta had become a Latin bishopric, and Benda, a chief town near Croia, was joined to it. The bishop thus held a double title, a common mark of sees that survived mainly on paper. The entry is a short thread in the tangled church map of the Balkans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bequest-for-m:
Bequests for Masses in Canada, gifts left in wills to pay for Masses for the dead, receive a legal entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Because property and civil rights fall to the provinces, no single Dominion rule governs such gifts. Each province's basic law decides whether a bequest for Masses stands.

Quebec, under French law from the cession of 1759 to 1763, raises no question of validity. Other provinces, working from English common law and statute, present a mixed picture the entry works through province by province. It is a lawyer's guide to a devotional gift caught in a federal system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethsaida:
Bethsaida, a city beside the Lake of Genesareth, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Its Aramaic name means house or place of fishing, and it was a frequent scene of Christ's preaching and miracles. Old writers knew only one Bethsaida, though they did not always point to the same site.

Since the sixteenth century scholars have debated whether two towns bore the name, one east of the Jordan and one west near Capernaum. The entry also notes a pool in Jerusalem called Bethesda in the Vulgate, and a titular see of the name. It is a careful sorting of places that share one Gospel name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-conra:
Blessed Conrad of Offida, a Franciscan friar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Offida about 1241, he died at Bastia in Umbria in 1306. Entering the Friars Minor at Ascoli at barely fourteen, he left study for humbler offices at an inner call, working for years as cook and questor, or begging brother.

Later ordained and sent to preach, his impassioned sermons touched the hardest hearts, and he allied with Angelo Clareno and the Spirituals, friars seeking Francis's rule in full purity. In 1294 Celestine V let him found the Celestines, suppressed by Boniface VIII, to whom Conrad then returned in obedience. He died on a mission at Bastia, and Perugians later carried his body to their cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-braganca-mira:
Braganca-Miranda, a Portuguese diocese in hilly Tras-os-Montes, lies between Spain's border and the Archdiocese of Braga. Its rivers run south from the Sanabria and Segundera ranges into the Duero, and its climate runs cold in the mountains. Low lands near Braganca grow grain, but much ground stays barren, though broad pastures feed herds that supply meat across Portugal and Spain.

Paul III erected the see at Miranda, on Spanish soil, from Braga's territory, and Clement XIV moved it to Braganca in 1770, giving the double name. Its cathedral of the Annunciation holds a large chapter of dean, nine canons, beneficed clergy, chaplains, and clerics. The palace and seminary stand large and spacious, and the fortified city counts a hospital and a Monte de piedad, besides schools of Christian doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-breda:
Breda, a Dutch diocese in Brabant suffragan to Utrecht, grew from a twelfth-century barony of the house of Nassau. Once under Liege, it passed to Antwerp when Pius IV raised that see in 1561. Iconoclasts scarred it in 1566, and Spanish and States-General troops traded it through decades of war until Frederick Henry took it finally on 10 October 1637.

Westphalia in 1648 left it under the States-General, where only the Reformed faith stood legal and Catholic worship survived in secret through zealous priests and faithful flocks. The Batavian Republic proclaimed worship free in 1796, and the 1815 constitution secured it. Pius VII created the Vicariate Apostolic of Breda in 1803 from Antwerp and Ghent lands, with Adrian van Dongen as first vicar and a seminary at Hoeven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calahorra-and:
Calahorra and la Calzada is a diocese under Burgos covering almost all of Logroño with parts of Navarre and Soria. Calahorra, its episcopal city of 9,475 people, honors the martyrs Emeterius and Celedonius, soldiers of the Seventh Legion, whose relics still rest in its cathedral. Its first known bishop is Silvanus, denounced to Pope Hilary about 465 for consecrating two bishops against the canons.

Mozarabic bishops held the see from 792 to 871, and after García of Navarre retook Calahorra the see was restored in 1045. In 1236 the see moved to Santo Domingo de la Calzada, so each town keeps a cathedral and chapter, and the bishop is chosen in turn by each chapter. The united dioceses count 65,000 Catholics in 363 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calynda:
Calynda was a titular see of Asia Minor, probably on the border of Lycia and Caria. Ptolemy places it in Lycia, and Stephanus of Byzantium places it in Caria and gives the form Karynda. It must not be confused with Kalydna, Kalydnos, Karyanda, or Kadyanda. Its king Damasithemos allied with Queen Artemisia, and the city struck coins under Rome.

Its Christian history is very short, and it never appears in the episcopal lists. All that is known is that it once answered to Myra, metropolis of Lycia, and that Bishop Leontius of Calynda signed the 458 letter of the Lycian bishops to Emperor Leo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canada:
Canada, the Dominion of Canada, takes in all of North America above the United States except Newfoundland, Labrador, and Alaska, spanning 3,000 miles from ocean to ocean and 3,745,574 square miles. A wide central plain lies between the western Cordilleran ranges, crowned by Mount Logan at 19,539 feet, and the eastern Laurentian plateau, a granite range at least 3,000 miles long.

The land's wealth runs to field crops, forests, fisheries, mines, manufactures, and commerce. Its peoples include the Indians, and its laws touch freedom of worship, the incorporation of bishoprics, taxation, wills, marriage, exemption for priests, and primary schooling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-indi:
Catholic missions among the Indigenous peoples of Canada began with the French explorers. When Jacques Cartier reached Baie des Chaleurs on 3 July 1534 he gave prayer beads to the people he met and raised a large cross. Two chaplains sailed on his second voyage. It ended with Donnacona, the Quebec chief carried off to France, accepting baptism.

Later foundations carried the work further. Priests sailed with the Sieur de Monts colony in Acadia in 1604. A few Micmacs were baptized by 1619, and Fathers Biard and Massé reached Port Royal in January 1611 to begin steady ministry among the neighboring peoples. The long article follows these missions through the tribes, orders, and stations of Canada down to its own day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholicity-i:
The story falls into three periods: French rule from Canada's discovery to the Treaty of Paris in 1763; British rule from 1763 onward; and present conditions. Basque, Breton, and Norman sailors may have raised the cross on Canadian shores before Cabot in 1497 or Verrazzano in 1522. They certainly came before Jacques Cartier, regarded as the country's discoverer.

Cartier made three voyages. On the first he had Mass celebrated at Gaspé in July 1534. On the second he went up the St. Lawrence, reached Stadacona, now Quebec, and pressed on to Hochelaga, the site of Montreal. Later sections cover the Acadians, schools in New Brunswick and Manitoba, Laval University at Montreal, colonization, the ecclesiastical provinces, religious orders, universities, and missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceneda:
Ceneda is a diocese in Treviso province, on land once Venetian, set on a slope of the Rhaetian Alps in picturesque country. Anciently it bore the names Ceneta or Acedum. Attila pillaged it in 452, and Totila did so a century later. Under the Lombards a duke governed it, and later it joined the marquisate of Treviso. From 994 the bishop of the city was also its temporal lord, keeping power over the city and a few villas until about 1768.

The Gospel is said to have reached the region in the first century through St. Fortunatus, a deacon of Hermagoras of Aquileia. The earliest known bishop, Vindemius, attended the Synod of Grado in 579, and Ursinus attended the Council of Rome in 680. Since 1818 Ceneda has been suffragan to Venice, counting 183,000 people, 118 parishes, and 500 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conradin-of-b:
John Volz's entry follows Conradin of Bornada, also of Brescia, Dominican preacher born late in the fourteenth century, died at Bologna on 1 November 1429. Noble Brescian parents, devoted adherents amid the Western Schism, gave him careful education. At sixteen he went to Padua for civil and canon law. Five years amid licence and disorder left him conspicuous for talent and virtue.

He entered the Dominicans at Padua in 1419, a model of observance. After ordination he preached with eloquent zeal. Prior of Brescia, then of Bologna's Saint Dominic convent, he restored strict observance. During plague he ministered with heroic zeal. When Bologna under the Bentivogli revolted against papal authority, he stood firm. Publishing the disregarded interdict brought two imprisonments with indignities. Courage and mediation restored peace. Martin V sought to make him cardinal, but he declined. Fresh plague claimed him amid ministrations, and early biographers call him Blessed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ar:
The Council of Aranda met in 1473 at Aranda in Burgos, summoned by Alfonso Carillo, Archbishop of Toledo, to confront ignorant and dissolute clergy. Spain's church in the late fifteenth century supplies the backdrop, with learning and morals both in decline. Twenty-nine canons answered that disorder, and one bars ordination for men ignorant of Latin.

Other canons take up clerical concubinage, simony, and clandestine marriages, the familiar abuses of a late medieval Spanish church. Together they sketch a reforming archbishop's programme: literate priests, clean hands in office, and marriages made openly under church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dhuoda:
A life of Dhuoda, wife of Bernard, Duke of Septimania, known only through her own book for her son. The Manual, begun at Uzès on 30 November 841 and finished 2 February 843, teaches her son William, born in 826, while she lived apart from husband and both sons. She married Bernard on 24 June 824, bore a second son in 841, and wrote, weak and near death, the epitaph she wished William to carve on her tomb.

Seventy-three chapters make the Manual a key source for general history and for the history of education, quite apart from its family counsel. Dhuoda may have died before her husband's condemnation for rebellion in 844 and before her sons' violent deaths in 850 and 872. Bondurand published the work in 1887 from a seventeenth-century manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edda:
Two different collections of old Norse literature bear the title Edda: the poetical Elder Edda and the prose Younger Edda. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the title properly belongs only to the younger work, reaching the elder by a misnomer. Snorri Sturluson, Icelandic historian and statesman of 1178 to 1241, wrote the Younger Edda.

It is a treatise on poetics meant to guide the skalds, the Icelandic poets. The title Edda stands in the most important manuscript, the Upsala Codex of about 1300. Its sense is unsure, though great-grandmother is now discarded and poetics is the reading most accepted. The entry points readers to Jonsson, Mogk, and Golther for the elder collection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinando-d-:
Ferdinando d'Adda was an Italian cardinal, diplomatist, and papal legate. Born at Milan in 1649, he was made cardinal-priest in 1690. He also served as prefect of the Congregation of Rites. Sent as nuncio to London under James II, he bore a delicate and dangerous diplomatic charge.

Innocent XI asked him to press King James to intercede with King Louis XIV. The royal plea sought relief for the oppressed Protestants of France. D'Adda later became cardinal-bishop of Albano in 1715. He died at Rome in 1719, after a long and distinguished career of diplomacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florida:
Florida is the most southern state in the American Union, named for Ponce de Leon's Easter landing in 1513. The peninsula runs 450 miles north to south, with a Gulf coast of 675 miles and an Atlantic coast of 470. The Everglades, wrongly called swamps, are submerged saw-grass plains fed by Lake Okeechobee. Pine woods, lakes, springs, and navigable rivers mark a well-watered, well-wooded land.

Farms in 1905 numbered over 45,000, with cotton, corn, fruit, and livestock leading output. The mild climate, with about 60 inches of rain yearly, made Florida a favourite winter resort. Forty-six counties divide the state, whose deep-water ports include Jacksonville, Tampa, and Key West. The St. John's, 300 miles long, and the Suwannee are among its chief rivers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-cep:
Francisco Cepeda, also called Zepeda, was born in La Mancha in 1532 and died at Guatemala in 1602, a Dominican missionary and pioneer of printing in the languages of America. He joined the Dominicans at Ocana and was sent to Chiapas in Mexico, where he worked actively among the Indians. When differing methods of teaching them hindered conversion, he was sent to Mexico to make the Indian grammars printed there simpler and set a standard for missionaries.

From that journey came the Artes de los idiomas Chiapanecos, Zoque, Tzendal y Chinanteco, published in 1560 under his name, probably the work of several authors. The book itself has disappeared, but its existence is well attested by Remesal and later writers, and it counts as the first American book printed in four languages, five counting Spanish. Cepeda later became provincial of the Dominicans in Guatemala in 1593 and commissary of the Inquisition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-:
Francisco de Moncada, Count of Osona, was a Spanish historian, soldier, and diplomat born at Valencia on 29 December 1586 and dead near Goch in Germany in 1635. Son of the governor of Sardinia and Catalonia, he entered the army very young. In 1624 Philip IV sent him as ambassador to the imperial court at Vienna, where he won the regard of Ferdinand II and his ministers. Recalled in 1629, he was sent to Brussels as ambassador to the Infanta Isabella, in place of Cardinal de la Cueva.

 He urged giving them a larger share, and even moving Belgian affairs from Madrid to Brussels, though without success. Made commander of the navy in 1630, of the whole army in 1632, and governor of Belgium in 1634, he freed Breda. Its citizens struck memorial coins in his honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fulda:
Fulda, a German diocese named for its ancient Benedictine abbey, began as Saint Boniface's base for winning the north. To reach the Saxons, Boniface sent Sturmius into the forest of Buchonia, where on March 12, 744, he took the land and raised the cross. The rule followed Monte Cassino, and Pope Zachary's privilege of 751 freed the abbey from all bishops save Rome.

Boniface asked to rest at Fulda, and his tomb made the abbey a national shrine for Christian Germany. Under Sturmius the monks cleared land, farmed, and planted daughter houses that grew into villages. Gifts from princes and nobles spread its estates from Thuringia to the Rhine and even to Rome. The article follows abbey, town, and diocese from forest clearing to imperial power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-malag:
Gabriel Malagrida, a Jesuit missionary to Brazil born in Italy in 1689, ended his life at an auto-da-fé in Lisbon in 1761. He entered the order at Genoa in 1711, reached Brazil in 1721, and labored twenty-eight years among its native peoples. Honored by King John V at Lisbon in 1749, he returned to Brazil, then came back to court at the queen dowager's wish.

His sway at court made him the target of Pombal, the prime minister, who had him banished to Setubal in 1756 and the Jesuits driven from court. After an attack that wounded the king by chance, Pombal built it into a Jesuit conspiracy with Malagrida at its head. Inquisition judges replaced by Pombal's men condemned him as heretic and dreamer, and he was strangled and burned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-granada:
Granada is an archdiocese in Spain, founded by Saint Cecilius about the year 64 and made an archiepiscopal see by Alexander VI on 23 January 1493. In the Roman period it appears as Municipium Florentinum Eliberritanum, and on coins as Ilurir, Iliber, Florentia, and Iliberri. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a city whose name changed under Arab rule.

Under the Arabs in the eighth century the old name gave way to Granada. It was originally the quarter inhabited since the third century by Jews, to whom the conquerors entrusted the city's custody. The tenth-century codex of San Millán lists sixty-two bishops of Elliberis, from Cecilius to Agapius. They span 64 to 957. On 15 May 301 the Council of Elliberis met at Granada with forty-three bishops present, including Hosius of Cordova.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guarda:
Portugal's Diocese of Guarda inherited the rank of ancient Idanha, the Roman city of Igaedi, when the see was re-established at Guarda in 1199 under Sancho I. Its bishops appear at the Second Council of Braga in 572, the see passed from Braga to Mérida after 666, and Moorish destruction in 715 closed its first chapter.

On revival, Innocent III settled a contest between Braga and Compostela in Compostela's favour, Lisbon took jurisdiction in 1490, and part of the territory went to form Portalegre in 1549. Notable bishops include Vasco Martins de Alvelha, who pressed for the Templars' absolution at Salamanca in 1310, and Pedro Vaz Gaviao, who finished Guarda's sumptuous cathedral. Nunho de Noronha founded its seminary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isionda:
A titular see of Pamphylia Secunda under Perge, Isionda survives in ancient geographers' pages more than in any story of its own. Artemidorus, quoted by Strabo, places it in Pisidia. Strabo himself puts Isinda near Termessos. Polybius, Ptolemy, and Stephen of Byzantium give the town other names: Isionda, Isindos, Pisinda, and Sinda. Church lists carry the same name in varied spellings.

Lequien names five bishops who attended the councils of Nicaea, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and Constantinople in 553, plus the Photian synod of 878. The town, which has no history of its own, probably stood at Istanoz or Stanos in the Adalia region. The entry is a detective note: a place known only because its bishops kept turning up at councils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-almeida:
John Almeida, born Meade in London in 1571, was a Jesuit missionary in Brazil who nearly equaled his master Anchieta in austerity and heroism. Taken to Portugal as a boy and adopted by the Rocha family, he sailed to Brazil at seventeen for trade. He survived a fall overboard he counted miraculous. Instead he entered the Society of Jesus at twenty-one, meeting Anchieta at Santo Spirito.

Ordained in 1602, he spent years on foot through the forests, seeking to convert fierce native peoples. He ate only what he gathered and refused to be carried however exhausted. Companions swore that for years he never tasted fish or flesh nor lay on a bed, spending nights sitting or kneeling in prayer. Hair shirts, iron chains, and spiked metal plates covered his body, yet his health held until his death at Rio de Janeiro in 1653, at eighty-two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-pined:
John de Pineda was a Spanish Jesuit exegete whose commentaries on Job and Solomon were praised by Catholic and Protestant scholars alike. Born at Seville in 1558, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1572 and taught philosophy and theology. He specialized in Scripture for eighteen years at Cordova, Seville, and Madrid. He became provost and rector at Seville and consultor to the Spanish Inquisition.

His Index of Prohibited Books of 1612, drawn from visits to Spain's chief libraries, won the Inquisition's appreciation. His thirteen-book commentary on Job, issued from 1597, paraphrases and comments on every chapter. It uses archaeology, textual criticism, and profane history, far ahead of its time in scientific criticism. His eight books on Solomon and his commentary on Ecclesiastes, with their many indices, show the same colossal erudition that made his fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josef-skoda:
Josef Skoda was a Bohemian-born doctor who helped build the modern Vienna medical school. Born at Pilsen in 1805, the son of a locksmith, he took his medical degree at Vienna in 1831. He worked through a cholera outbreak and rose to professor of the medical clinic in 1846. In 1848 he became the first Vienna professor to lecture in German rather than Latin.

Skoda's fame rests on physical diagnosis: tapping the chest, called percussion, and listening to the body, called auscultation. His short 1839 treatise on those methods, reprinted and translated many times, made his name known worldwide. He also pushed for reform of medical study and gave much of his income to charity, leaving only a small fortune.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-carreno-:
Juan Carreño de Miranda was a Spanish court painter of the age of Velázquez. Born at Avilés in Asturias in 1614, he studied under Pedro de Las Cuevas and Bartolomé Román, but by twenty he knew more than his masters and opened his own studio. Velázquez helped him study the royal palace frescoes, and in 1660 the king made him court painter.

Carreño kept the post under Charles II, painting three lifelike portraits of the child-king and a strong full-length Potemkin, the Russian ambassador, in red. His work is tender, suave, and freshly colored, second only to Murillo in manner, though his portraits echo Velázquez' poses too closely. With Ricci he decorated the cupola of San Antonio de los Portugueses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-martinez:
Juan Martínez de Ripalda was a Spanish Jesuit theologian ranked with Lugo among Spain's finest. Born at Pamplona in 1594, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1609 and taught grammar, arts, and theology for nineteen years. He held Salamanca's theology chair with more honor, Drews says, than any Jesuit before him. Royal decree then called him to Madrid's Imperial College.

Ripalda served as censor to the Inquisition and confessor to Olivares, Philip IV's favorite, following him into exile. Hurter places him first among contemporary Spanish theologians. His works argue that a supernatural substance is possible, that grace attends every good act, and that Mary's divine motherhood itself sanctifies. He died at Madrid in 1648.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juda:
Juda is at once a patriarch, a tribe, and a territory in the Old Testament. Juda, son of Jacob by Leah, took his name from the Hebrew word for praise, spoken at his birth. He saved Joseph's life by urging his sale to Ishmaelites rather than murder, and later offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place before Joseph.

The tribe of Juda, largest at the Exodus with 74,600 fighting men at the first census, gave Israel Caleb the spy and its kings through the line of Phares. The entry traces the name from the patriarch through the tribe's numbers and leaders to the land it held, and notes the other Old Testament men who bore the name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laranda:
Laranda was a titular see of Isauria, later of Lycaonia. Strabo notes it belonged to Antipater of Derbe, suggesting native princes ruled it, and Perdiccas stormed and destroyed it before it was rebuilt.

Fertile land made it one of the district's chief cities and a pirate centre of Isauria, and it bore the poets Nestor and his son Pisander. Later it joined the Konia sultanate, became capital of Caramania after the Seljuk division, and fell to Sultan Bayezid II in 1486. Now generally called Caraman, it holds about 15,000 people, mostly Muslims, makes cotton and silk cloth, and stands as a railway station between Konia and Eregli toward Baghdad. Four bishops are known, from Neo to Sabbas at Constantinople in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lerida:
Lerida, the diocese of Ilerdensis, is suffragan of Tarragona. La Canal dates it to 600; others trace it to the third century, with St. Lycerius named bishop in A.D. 269. Bishops' signatures run through councils up to 716, when the Moors took the town and the see moved to Roda, then in 1101 to Barbastro.  Lerida, Roman Ilerda, Catalonia's second city, stands on the Segre about 100 miles from Barcelona.

In the Punic wars it sided with Carthage. Near it Hanno lost to Scipio in 216 B.C., and Caesar beat Pompey's army in 49 B.C. The Moors held it from 716 until Berenger drove them out in 1149. France held it in 1810 during the Peninsular War, and Spain regained it in 1823. Strongly fortified, it had narrow, crooked streets and 23,683 people in 1900. The old cathedral ruins on the citadel date from 1203.   The seminary, founded in 1722, holds 500 students, and the diocese counts 185,000 Catholics in 395 parishes served by 598 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-de-lossa:
Luis de Lossada was a Spanish Jesuit philosopher, born at Quiroga in 1681 and dead at Salamanca in 1748. He joined the Society in 1698 and taught theology, Scripture, and philosophy at Salamanca with great success.

His Dialectical Institutions of 1721, called Summulae, led into his great Course of Philosophy of the Royal College of Salamanca, published in 1724 and reprinted in ten volumes at Barcelona in 1883. It covers all philosophy with learning and clarity, following Suarez with some departures, and Urraburu admired and followed it closely. Lossada also wrote on St. Dominic's descent for the Bollandists, and his satiric vein once earned him credit for Isla's Fray Gerundio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lydda:
Lydda is a titular see of Palestina Prima in the Jerusalem patriarchate, first called Lod and founded by Samad of Benjamin. Its people went captive to Babylon and returned. Syrian kings gave the town to the Maccabees until Pompey came to Judea, after which Caesar, Cassius, and Antony in turn held, sold, and freed its folk.

Christians lived here from the first, and Peter cured the paralytic Aeneas on a visit, recorded in Acts. A council in December 415 absolved Pelagius while condemning his errors, and the town took the name Georgiopolis for St. George, said its native son, whose tomb church Crusaders rebuilt. Today 6,800 live there, mostly Muslims and schismatic Greeks, with a small Catholic parish nearby at Ramleh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marco-girolam:
Marco Girolamo Vida was an Italian humanist, born at Cremona about 1490 and dead in 1566. He reached Rome under Julius II, a priest and canon regular famed for strict morals in a lax court. Humanists were asked for a great Christian epic, and Leo X gave him the priory of St Sylvester at Frascati to write it.

The Christiade was finished after Leo's death and printed at Cremona in 1535. In six cantos, free of myth, it runs beyond Christ's life to the spread of Christianity, and so is more unified than Sannazaro's poem on the Virgin's birth. Vida also wrote short poems on silk and chess and a long didactic poem, De arte poetica, written before 1520 and printed in 1527. It trains a poet from childhood in invention, composition, and style, praising Virgil above Homer and shaping classical teaching through Virgil examples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-de-agre:
Marie de Agreda, Maria of Jesus by convent title, was a discalced Franciscan nun, born in 1602 and dead on 24 May 1665. Her family name was Coronel, and Agreda names the Old Castile town where an ancestor was said to have built a convent at a revelation's command.

Her fame rests on the Mystical City of God, a life of Mary drawn from claimed revelations. It drew little notice outside Spain until Croset, a Recollect friar, translated its first part at Marseilles in 1696, sparking a storm, above all in the Sorbonne. The Sorbonne studied it through July 1696 in thirty-two sessions and censured it that October. It faulted its weight on new revelations, its use of adoration for Mary, its claim that Mary governed the Church, and its Scotist theses dressed as revelation. Bossuet denounced it, Thomists blamed Scotist partisanship, and foes still honoured her holy life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massa-candida:
Massa Candida, the White Mass, were three hundred holy martyrs at Carthage under Valerian and Gallienus, commemorated 24 August in the Roman Martyrology. The governor lit a limekiln, set live coals with incense nearby, and told the confessors to choose incense to Jupiter or the lime. Armed with faith and confessing Christ, they hurled themselves with one swift impulse into the fire, where burning lime fumes reduced them to powder.

The event falls between 253, when Gallienus joined his father as emperor, and 260, when Valerian fell prisoner to Persia's Sapor. Augustine calls them the White Mass of Utica, twenty-five miles from Carthage, where they were specially honoured. The three hundred may have come from Utica for trial by procurator Galerius Maximus. Hence the band earned forever the name Massa Candida.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-merida:
Merida, a suffragan see of Santiago of Venezuela, or Caracas, covers the State of Los Andes with parts of Zulia and Zamora. Until 1905 it also held the Goajira territory. Merida became a bishopric in 1777. Its first bishop, Juan Ramos de Lora, a Franciscan born at Palacios y Villafranca in Seville's diocese in 1722, was named in the consistory of 23 September 1782. He served as suffragan of Santa Fe de Bogota.

His successors came swiftly: Emanuelo Candido de Terrissos in 1791, Antonio Espinosa of Corvera in 1795, and Jaime Hernandez Milanes of Nieza, named by Pius VII in 1801. By that pope's bull In Universalis Ecclesiae of 24 October 1803, Merida became suffragan to Caracas, just raised to an archdiocese. In 1816 Rafael Laso de La Vega was elected bishop. Amid rebellion against Spain, Leo XII named Bonaventura Arias auxiliary in 1826. Arias governed after Laso moved to Quito in 1828.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nevada:
Nevada, a western American state, borders Oregon and Idaho in the north, Utah and Arizona in the east, and California in the south and west. It spans latitudes 35 to 42 north and longitudes 114 to 120, stretching 483 miles north to south and 320 east to west, with a total area of 110,590 square miles. Its climate is dry, pleasant and healthful, with very warm summers except in high mountains and long, sometimes severe winters.

A warm westerly wind in late spring and early autumn often brings disastrous sandstorms. January averages 28 degrees, summer 71, and yearly rainfall averages ten inches, mostly from December to May. Population history since 1850 fascinates: from a few hundred pioneers to 60,000 in the mining boom years of 1860 to 1880, then decline after 1885. The entry covers the state's mines, railways, towns, and the Catholic Church's missions, parishes and bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicephorus-bl:
Nicephorus Blemmida, or Blemmydes, was a learned monk and writer of the Greek Church, born about 1198 at Constantinople and dead in 1272. After the Latin Empire's establishment in 1204, his family emigrated to Asia Minor, where he received careful training and soon ranked among his time's most learned men. About 1223 he joined the Byzantine clergy then established at Nicaea.

Difficulties and jealousies made him renounce worldly prospects, become a monk, and build a monastery near Ephesus, which he led until death. Free from entanglements, he showed independence and courage, dismissing Princess Marcesina, Emperor John Ducas Batatzes's mistress, from his monastery church and justifying himself by encyclical letter. He likewise refused Patriarch Joseph's bid for recognition against former Patriarch Arsenius. Emperors esteemed him highly, and Theodore II offered him Constantinople's patriarchate in 1255, which he declined.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olinda:
Olinda, a Brazilian diocese suffragan to Bahia, now covers the state of Pernambuco from its seat at Recife. Paul V made it a vicariate in 1614, Innocent XI raised it to a bishopric in 1676, and Leo XIII carved Paraíba in 1892 and Alagoas in 1900 from its lands.

Duarte Coelho founded Olinda in 1534, the Dutch held it from 1630 to 1654 and built Moritzstadt, now Recife, nearby, and the bishop's residence later moved to Recife's Boa Vista quarter. Its most noted prelate, Thomas of the Incarnation, wrote a history of the Portuguese church. Recife, now the residence quarter of Boa Vista, holds a university and five hospitals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-aranda:
Philip Aranda was an Aragonese Jesuit theologian, born at Moneva in 1642. He entered the Society in 1658 and taught theology and philosophy at Saragossa. Father Michel de St. Joseph praised him as most acute in theology, eloquent in speech, and a practised athlete of the scholastic arena. His 1693 treatise On God Knowing, Predestining, and Helping examines middle knowledge and expounds predestination and grace.

Aranda explained Augustine's hard sayings with ease, insisting they never touched predestination, a word he claimed the Doctor never used even in equivalent terms. An appendix asks why the Second Person's procession is called generation. He also wrote on incarnation, redemption, human acts, good and evil, and a life of Isabel Pobar. A Dominican satire calling his work olla podrida nearly drew an interdict on its author's church. He died at Saragossa in 1695.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolf-of-ful:
Rudolf of Fulda, chronicler, died at Fulda on 8 March 862. In Fulda monastery he entered the Benedictine Order, studied under Rabanus Maurus, and became a teacher. He worked with King Louis the Pious and counted himself the king's close friend. Probably after Rabanus became Archbishop of Mainz, Rudolf followed him there. He was among the most distinguished scholars of his time.

The Annals of Fulda, begun by Einhard and continued by Rudolf from 838 to 863, are valuable for the period's history. At Rabanus's suggestion, Rudolf in 838 compiled a life of St Lioba from the priest Mego's notes and oral tradition. Under a misleading title about Rabanus, a work survives on miracles of relics brought to Fulda, with historical and ethnological notes. More important is his Translatio of St Alexander to Wildeshausen in 851, begun in 863 and completed by Meginhart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacred-congre:
The Sacred Congregation de Propaganda Fide, for spreading the Christian name, is the pope's department for spreading the faith and ruling church affairs in non-Catholic lands. Its great duties and wide rule have made its cardinal prefect known as the red pope. It was set up at Rome in the seventeenth century, partly to reach newly found lands, and partly from the new system of rule by congregations in the Counter-Reformation.

Defence and spread of the faith suggested a full system of departments, each given some special branch of church interests. The Faith's spread demanded an entire congregation. Winning back lost lands mattered no more than preaching in vast new regions found by bold explorers. America, Africa, and the Far East opened new lands and peoples. The Church, mindful of her task to preach to the world, felt she must act fast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-ca:
Saint John is the New Brunswick diocese in Canada, taking in Albert, Carleton, Charlotte, Kings, Queens, Saint John, Sunbury, Westmoreland, and York counties, with part of Kent. Its chief city, the oldest incorporated city in British North America, chartered in 1785, is also the largest city in the province. Among the earliest Catholic missionaries to the region, then part of Acadia, were the Jesuits Biard and Massé in 1611, followed by Recollects after Port Royal was destroyed in 1613.

Bishop Saint Vallier reached Medoctec, an Indian village below Woodstock, in 1686 and set up a mission under the Recollect Father Simon, later passing to Jesuits including Loyard and Germain. A stone tablet found in 1890 records that the Maliseets built the Medoctec church in 1717 while Jean Loyard was procurator of the mission. French Catholic settlers arrived after the treaties of 1632 and 1667, becoming the ancestors of the Acadians spread over New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alfrida:
St. Alfrida was a virgin and recluse of about 795, daughter of Offa, King of Mercia, and this entry is candid about the shaky ground beneath her story.
