Her name appears in many spellings, Elfthritha, Aelfleda, Alfritha, and more. And the late, not very trustworthy legend says she was betrothed to Ethelbert, King of the East Angles, murdered by treachery at Offa's court when he came to claim her.

After the murder Alfrida withdrew to the marshes of Crowland, where she was walled into a cell and lived as a recluse to the end of her days. The entry warns of likely confusion with Aelfleda, another daughter of Offa whose husband was also murdered by treachery. And readers get a saint whose history is mostly a caution about legends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ceadda:
St. Ceadda, commonly known as St. Chad, was abbot of Lastingham and bishop successively of York and Lichfield in England. This entry follows a man of uncertain birth date who died in 672. His brother St. Cedd — also abbot of Lastingham and bishop of the East Saxons — is often confused with him. Two other brothers, Cynibill and Caelin, also became priests. Likely Northumbrian by birth, he learned at Lindisfarne under St. Aidan.

Afterwards he went to Ireland, where he studied with St. Ecgberht at Rathmelsige, or Melfont. He then returned to help his brother Cedd establish Laestingaeu, now Lastingham in Yorkshire. When his brother died in 664, he took over as abbot. Shortly afterwards St. Wilfrid, chosen to succeed Tudi as bishop of Lindisfarne, went to Gaul for consecration. He remained so long absent that King Oswiu waited no longer, and procured Chad's election as bishop of York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cedd-cedda:
St. Cedd, or Cedda, was bishop of the East Saxons and brother of St. Ceadda. He died on 26 October 664. This entry follows a man with two other priest brothers, Cynibill and Caelin, born to an Angle family settled in Northumbria. He grew up at Lindisfarne under St. Aidan with his younger brother Ceadda. In 653 he was one of four priests Oswiu, king of Northumbria, sent to evangelize the Middle Angles at their ealdorman Peada's request.

Shortly after, however, he was recalled and sent on the same errand to Essex, to help Sigeberht, king of the East Saxons, convert his people to Christ. There he was consecrated bishop, founded churches with great energy, and established monasteries at Tilbury and Ithancester. Occasionally he revisited his native Northumbria. There, at Aethelwald's request, he founded the monastery of Laestingaeu, now Lastingham in Yorkshire, and became its first abbot despite his episcopal rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clotilda:
St. Clotilda, French Clotilde, German Chlothilde, was queen of the Franks, born, it seems, at Lyons about 474. She died at Tours on 3 June 545, and her feast is kept 3 June. This entry follows the wife of Clovis I and daughter of Chilperic, king of the Burgundians of Lyons, and Caretena. After King Gundovic's death, Burgundy was split among his four sons: Chilperic ruled at Lyons, Gondebad at Vienne, and Godegisil at Geneva.

Chilperic was Catholic, and Godegisil likely so; Gondebad professed Arianism. Her mother Caretena gave Clotilda a training in the faith; Sidonius Apollinaris and Fortunatus of Poitiers praise Caretena. After Chilperic's death, Caretena settled with Godegisil at Geneva, where her other daughter, Sedeleuba, or Chrona, founded Saint-Victor's church and took a nun's habit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ethelreda:
Ethelreda, queen of Northumbria and foundress of Ely, guarded a religious vocation through two political marriages. Born about 630 to Anna, king of East Anglia, she was wed young to Tonbert, who gave her the Isle of Ely as morning gift. She never lived in wedlock with him, and after his early death spent five years fostering her calling. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Ely to 23 June 679.

Her father then married her to Egfrid, heir of Northumbria, a boy said to be only fourteen. Through Wilfrid of York she gave Hexham lands to found St. Andrew's minster. When Egfrid, now king, pressed his marital rights, Wilfrid first won him to let her live as a sister in religion. The entry follows a queen turning royal gifts into monastic ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hilda:
Hilda, abbess of Whitby, turned a Northumbrian monastery into a school that produced five bishops. Born in 614 to Hereric, nephew of King Edwin, she became Christian about 627, aged thirteen, through Paulinus's preaching, as her great-uncle had. Her sister Hereswitha became a nun at Chelles after marrying East Anglia's king. Moved by her example, Hilda set out for East Anglia intending to follow her abroad. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 680.

Aidan recalled her home. After monastic life on the Wear's north bank and at Hartlepool, she ruled a double house of monks and nuns with great success. Then she ordered the monastery at Streaneshalch, later Whitby. There Scripture was specially studied, and five inmates became bishops. Practically all knowledge of Hilda comes from Bede, and the entry trusts his pages for a ruler, teacher, and founder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-matilda:
Matilda, queen of Germany and wife of Henry I the Fowler, rose from a Westphalian monastery school to the centre of tenth-century politics. Born about 895 at Engern, she married Henry in 909 and bore children who shaped Europe, including the emperor Otto I and Bruno, archbishop of Cologne. As queen she was known for humility, generosity, and a steady hand on her husband.

After Henry died in 936, she backed her favourite son Henry for the throne against the chosen heir Otto, and watched Henry revolt and submit. Widowed and wealthy, she poured her lands into churches and poor relief, founded houses at Quedlinburg and elsewhere, and died there on 14 March 968. The entry blends court politics with a portrait of royal piety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synnada:
Synnada was a titular metropolis in Phrygia Salutaris, said to have been founded by Acamas after the Trojan War with Macedonian colonists. The consul Manlius Vulso passed through it campaigning against the Galatians. Lying in southeastern Phrygia at the foot of Pisidia's mountains, it belonged to the Attalid kingdom, then became capital of a district of Asia, with brief spells attached to Cilicia.

Under both regimes it hosted an important judicial assembly, which Cicero attended travelling between Ephesus and Cilicia. Though small, it won empire-wide fame for marble from nearby Dacimium's quarries. Under Diocletian it became a metropolis at the crossing of two great roads, and today it is Schifout Kassaba, where a third-century sarcophagus reliquary of St Trophimus was found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-spanish-a:
Spain's great fleet against England, the Invincible Armada or more rightly La Armada Grande, is the subject of this naval history. It aimed to invade England and end long English attacks on Spanish colonies and possessions, yet a week's fighting and a disastrous cruise all but destroyed it. Spain's sea power then faded gradually, the entry's third point.

Philip had begun as Elizabeth's best friend, saving her life after Wyatt's rebellion, easing her accession, and backing her against Mary Stuart and France. English raids and religious war soured the friendship. Catholics mostly supported the Armada, with notable exceptions, and the entry weighs causes, battles, wreck, and aftermath with even hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thebes-achaia:
Boeotian Thebes, founded by Phoenician Cadmus in the sixteenth century before Christ, is the ancient city surveyed here as a metropolitan titular see of Achaia Secunda. Legends of Laius, Oedipus, and Antigone, rivalry of Eteocles and Polynices, and the seven chiefs' siege made it illustrious. After Troy's fall it became Boeotia's capital, yet Athens backed rivals against its hegemony.

Alliance with Persia against Greeks brought conquest and submission to Sparta, until Pelopidas and Epaminondas restored Thebes to first rank. Epaminondas's death before Mantinea in 363 opened fresh misfortunes: Philip of Macedon conquered it in 338, Alexander razed it two years later, sparing only Pindar's house, and Cassander rebuilt it in 316.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thebes-thebai:
Egyptian Thebes, No-Amon to Jews and Diospolis to Greeks, is the titular see of Thebais Secunda described here, suffragan of Ptolemais and seat of a Coptic Catholic diocese. Egyptians called it Nouit-Amen, City of Amon, and Per or Pi-Amen, dwelling of Amon, with Apet giving, through Ta-Apet or Tape, the Copts' name and the Greeks' Thebai. Bible mentions it thrice as No-Amon, wrongly rendered Alexandria in the Vulgate.

Nahum chapter 3 recalls Assurbanipal's victories over Tanutamen, while Jeremiah and Ezechiel allude to Nabuchodonosor's campaigns of 583 and 588 before Christ. From mere borough it rose to imperial capital, its temples and tombs still bearing witness to ancient glory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-malven:
Thomas Malvenda, an exegete and historical critic, was born at Jativa, Valencia, in 1566 and died in 1628. He entered the Dominicans young and was teaching philosophy and theology by thirty-five. His criticisms of Baronius's Annals, sent in a letter of 1600, impressed Baronius so much that he had Malvenda summoned to Rome.

At Rome Malvenda advised the cardinal, helped revise the Dominican Breviary, and annotated the Index Expurgatorius. His Antichristo appeared in 1604 and his work on Paradise in 1605. Back in Spain from 1608, he began a word-for-word Latin version of the Old Testament from Hebrew, with commentaries. He had reached Ezekiel 16 when he died, and the work appeared at Lyons in 1650.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tomas-de-torq:
Tomas de Torquemada, first Grand Inquisitor of Spain, was born at Valladolid in 1420 and died at Avila in 1498. Nephew of the cardinal and theologian Juan de Torquemada, he entered the Dominicans at Valladolid and served twenty-two years as prior of Santa Cruz at Segovia. The Infanta Isabella chose him as confessor there, and after her accession in 1474 he became one of her most trusted councillors, refusing high church office to stay a simple friar.

Sixtus IV empowered the Catholic monarchs to set up the Inquisition in 1478, but it faltered for want of central direction. In 1483 the pope named Torquemada Grand Inquisitor of Castile, extending his power to Aragon that October. He then directed the whole Spanish Inquisition, delegating his powers to inquisitors of his own choice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Granada's university traces its origin to the Arab school at Cordova, moved to Granada when St Ferdinand captured Cordova in 1236. When Granada itself fell to the Catholic sovereigns, their early care was to preserve letters and the art of teaching, in which the Arabs had excelled. The school passed under their protection. Yet it gained university status only under Charles V, when Clement VII issued a bull of erection dated 1531.

The new institution held privileges like those of Bologna, Paris, Salamanca, and Alcalá. Its large building, raised by the Jesuits, suited its purpose admirably, the entry notes. The account follows its faculties and fortunes through later centuries, offering a compact history of a school that carried Arab learning into Christian Spain and then into a Spanish university.

St Joseph's at Memramcook, New Brunswick, was founded in 1864 by Father Camille Lefebvre of the Congregation of Holy Cross. Its rise owed much to Bishop Sweeny of St John, who wanted the youth of his diocese, and especially the French Acadians in his care, to gain secondary schooling. The college was incorporated, with power to grant degrees, by an act of the New Brunswick legislature in 1868, and thirty years later an amendment gave it its present title.

Besides faculties of arts and theology, commercial courses in English and French always held a firm place in its curriculum. The entry credits St Joseph's with much of the advance of French-speaking people in Canada's Maritime Provinces over the past half-century. It sketches a small college whose teaching in two tongues served a community long short of schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-louis-of-:
Louis of Granada was a theologian, writer, and preacher born of very humble parents at Granada in Spain in 1505, who died at Lisbon on 31 December 1588. At nineteen he joined the Dominican Order at Santa Cruz in Granada. A mind of the highest quality, unremitting application, and a deeply spiritual character promised him a brilliant and fruitful career in the church's service.

Once his philosophy studies were done, his superiors chose him to represent his convent at the College of St Gregory in Valladolid. That Dominican house was reserved for students of more than ordinary ability. There he shone with rare distinction, not only in church courses but in the humanities, which he pursued at his superiors' request. The entry follows his preaching, his writings, and his fame as a spiritual master.
catholic-problems-in-western-canada:
George Thomas Daly, a Redemptorist priest, published his study of western Canada at Toronto in 1921, with a preface by O. E. Mathieu, Archbishop of Regina, and a dedication to the Catholic hierarchy of Canada. Eighteen chapters divide into religious, educational, and social problems facing the Church across the fast-settling West.

Daly argues for the Catholic Church Extension Society, a field secretary, and work among Ukrainian (Ruthenian) settlers and non-Catholics. School chapters defend separate schools and a fair split of company taxes, and urge a Catholic university for the West. Later chapters take up postwar rebuilding, public opinion, the press, and new immigrants. Eastern help for western missions is the plea running through it.
daniel-deronda:
George Eliot's Daniel Deronda is her last great novel, in eight books from The Spoiled Child to Fruit and Seed. Its epigraph warns that one's own soul should be the chief terror, since desires crowd and crush in their scramble for spoils.

Gwendolen, the spoiled child, meets streams of influence that carry her toward Deronda, Mordecai, revelations, and a mother and son reunited. Eliot weaves English society, Jewish identity and moral choice into a single, searching narrative. Readers who know Middlemarch will find Deronda more sombre and more daring, and newcomers will find a masterpiece of Victorian moral fiction.
doe-osti-2583497-sam-linear-fresnel-mode:
Project B of a long-running agreement between NREL and the Electric Power Research Institute is closed out in report NREL/TP-6A20-94643, dated April 11, 2025. Ty Neises was the laboratory's contact. EPRI adopted NREL's Solar Advisor Model back in 2010. It became the default tool for judging solar thermal plants. But one technology had no neutral model anywhere: linear Fresnel. Fresnel plants focus sunlight with long rotating mirror strips. The light lands on a fixed linear receiver.

Vendor software can model a vendor's plant, but utilities and investors need an umpire. Project B built the Fresnel performance and cost model inside SAM, NREL's public tool. Any funder can now test claims on their own. The work matters because solar developers increasingly pitch Fresnel layouts as cheaper options than troughs and towers. With the model in SAM, those pitches face the same financial checks applied to every other solar thermal design.
doe-osti-2585400-next-generation-sensor-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-873258 is the final report for a cooperative research and development agreement on next generation sensors. Brian Wihl authored the report, and Kerry Krauter and Wihl served as principal investigators. The partner was the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, with the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond also involved. Technical work ended on December 31, 2023.

Under CRADA number TC02281, the team developed sensing and image analysis methods tied to the Federal Reserve's currency work. One thread built an algorithm to judge fitness and soiling levels from images. Simple average differences between input and output images proved inadequate for grading soiling. The team therefore adopted the structural similarity index measure, which quantified image differences more usefully. The report closes out the agreement and records what the collaboration produced.
doe-osti-2588294-a-review-of-regulations:
Michael Devin, Marina Miletic, and Brian Ehrhart of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this review, SAND2025-11072, of the regulations, codes, and standards that govern hydrogen fuel cell electric buses on airports. Airports want zero-emission shuttle and transit buses, but hydrogen brings fueling stations, maintenance shops, and safety rules written for other settings.

The review collects the documents that actually apply, then runs a gap analysis against airport use. Fueling follows SAE J2601-2, the heavy duty hydrogen fueling protocol. Facility rules cover layouts and siting for maintenance buildings and how many dispensers a fleet needs. One code chapter's provisions on bonding and grounding, electrical equipment setback distances, and emergency shutdown locations are flagged as directly applicable. Where the documents were written for general industry rather than airports, the analysis names the mismatch, so transit agencies and airport operators can plan compliance instead of discovering gaps later.
doe-osti-3018281-2026-large-load-literat:
Vinita Srinivasan and Natalie Mims Frick of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory compiled this large load literature review, updated September 2026. It is a living document, reissued as the field moves. Large loads, the data centers and industrial sites now straining grid planning, are its subject. The review began in 2025 with more than ninety publications, sorted into twelve themes.

The 2026 round reviewed forty-one more publications under the same themes: load forecasting, artificial intelligence infrastructure, reliability, interconnection, demand flexibility, tariffs, and policy among them. Each entry is linked, with a short description and key takeaways, newest first. Since September 2025 a data sources section flags which reports rest on named data, marked with an asterisk. One cited line of work focuses on distribution-connected loads of one to twenty megawatts, a different beast from hyperscale campuses. Planners get a maintained map of a literature growing faster than anyone can read.
doe-osti-3020680-evaluations-of-connecto:
Report DOE/GO-102025-6935, by Marco Gaxiola, Isaac Tolbert, Andrew Meintz, and Kristi Moriarty, dated February 20, 2026, measures the physical forces at electric vehicle charging plugs. Funded by the Joint Office of Energy and Transportation, the study covers direct-current fast-charging connectors and vehicle inlets. It also covers the adapters drivers now use between the SAE J3400 North American Charging Standard and the older J1772 standard. Heavy cables and adapters act as lever arms on the connection.

The team replicated the side-load tests in the UL 2251 and IEC 62196-1 standards, including the 100-newton misalignment check and the 750-newton withstand check. Across three vehicle and charger positions, mated forces stayed below the 100-newton limit, but in the most stretched position, with cables pulled to their limit, forces exceeded recommendations. The report closes with recommendations for standards and hardware design.
doe-osti-3364259-uniform-methods-project:
A slide deck from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, presented by Christian Jewett and Chuck Kurnik at a February 25, 2026 webinar, updates the Uniform Methods Project. The project maintains shared protocols for measuring gross energy savings from ratepayer-funded efficiency programs. Before it existed, seventeen technical reference manuals covered 21 states plus Washington, D.C., and the same measure could yield wildly different savings numbers under each.

The deck reviews the project's history and its library of measure protocols, from lighting and furnaces to retrocommissioning and data centers. Planned 2026 work moves into a maintenance phase, adds peak demand savings, and takes up newer measurement and verification approaches. A technical advisory group guides the updates. The audience is regulators, program administrators, and evaluators who need savings figures they can compare across states.
doe-osti-3380281-maturation-of-next-gene:
Maturation of Next Generation eSAF, CRADA final report NLR/TP-5100-98565 from July 2026, closes out Project 2 under agreement CRD-24-25166. The National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts are Gary Grim and Ling Tao, the cited authors. Funding was provided by the Department of Energy's Office of Electricity, an unusual sponsor pairing the report itself records.

eSAF is electro-fuel sustainable aviation fuel, jet fuel synthesized with electricity-driven chemistry rather than refined from petroleum or made only from biomass. Maturation work in a CRADA of this kind moves a process from laboratory proof toward reliable, repeatable production: better yields, steadier operation, and data a commercial partner can build on. The report stands as the final record of Project 2's share of that effort.
doe-osti-3409097-building-operation-mode:
In August 2026, the National Laboratory of the Rockies released report NLR/TP-5500-99927, which covers Morpheus, a building operation model for Dallas Fort Worth Airport. Korbaga Woldekidan was the lab contact, with Sarah K. Ziomek in the evidence record. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-19-16301.

Morpheus uses a grey-box model tuned with airport data. Terminal loads hinge on occupancy, work processes, and outside loads such as electric ground support gear. A partner system called Athena supplies occupancy data through information exchange. Airport staff can test control choices in the model before changing real heating and cooling systems.
doe-osti-3484709-electromagnetic-transie:
In August 2026, the National Laboratory of the Rockies released report NLR/TP-5D00-101189, which models electromagnetic transients from data centers. Shahil Shah and Weihang Yan of the Rockies lab wrote with Sabarish Kalyanaraman of Texas Instruments. Data center power gear switches fast and can disturb grid studies.

A double-averaged model skips detailed control simulation for speed. It stays valid below a few hundred hertz, the text states. That range is about one tenth of the control bandwidth. A bulk capacitor voltage controller design follows from the model. Grid modelers can include data centers in fast transient studies without huge run times.
drake-s-great-armada:
Captain Walter Biggs sailed with Sir Francis Drake in 1585, and Drake's Great Armada preserves his account of that expedition, here in a 1910 New York edition. England and Spain were sliding toward open war. Queen Elizabeth licensed reprisals against Spanish shipping. A company of adventurers fitted out twenty-five ships and about 2,300 men under Drake's command.

An introduction traces the fleet from Plymouth to the Canaries and Cape Verde islands. The English burned Santiago, crossed the Atlantic in eighteen days, and reached the Caribbean. On New Year's Day 1586 they took Santo Domingo and held it for ransom. Biggs writes as a participant in raids on Spanish America. Readers get an early English sea narrative, proud, violent, and close to the events it describes.
dutt-ramayana-aranya-kanda:
Aranya Kandam, the forest book, comes in Dutt's 1892 English version. Rama's exile years pass among hermits, beasts, and lurking demons. Peace in the woods breaks when desire and spite enter the grove.

A demoness's rage brings her brother's armies against the exiles in vain. Then Ravana, the demon king, seizes Sita by trick and flight. He carries her to Lanka, and the epic's great quest begins. Dutt's prose keeps the forest book's beauty and terror both intact. Readers feel the tale turn from calm exile to vast cosmic war ahead. The forest itself seems to hold its breath in these chapters.
dutt-ramayana-ayodhya-kanda:
Ayodhya Kandam, in Dutt's 1892 English, forms the Ramayana's second book. Rama, crown prince of Ayodhya, stands ready to take the throne. A queen's old boon then sends him to the forest instead.

Rama gives up the crown to keep his father's sworn word. Sita and Lakshmana choose exile with him over ease at court. The city mourns, the old king dies of grief, and Bharata refuses rule. Duty wars with love in scene after moving scene here. Many readers call this book the emotional heart of the whole vast epic. Its scenes of parting are retold wherever the Ramayana is loved.
dutt-ramayana-bala-kanda:
Manmatha Nath Dutt gave English readers a prose Ramayana in the 1890s. His Bala Kanda, the Book of Childhood, appeared in 1892 translation. Rama's birth and youth open India's great epic in this volume.

The childless king's rite, the boys' schooling, and a sage's plea fill the tale. Young Rama slays demons and wins Sita by bending the great bow. Wonder, duty, and first love shine through Dutt's faithful prose rendering. His work was the first full English Ramayana of its kind. Readers meet the epic's bright dawn before exile darkens the road ahead. The book's wonder sets up all the sorrow to come.
dutt-ramayana-kishkindha-kanda:
Kishkindha Kandam, in Dutt's 1891 English, brings Rama to the monkey kingdom. Grieving for Sita, he meets the exiled monkey king Sugriva there. Their pact of friendship sets the search for Sita in motion.

Rama helps Sugriva win back his throne from his brother Vali. Monkey hosts then fan out across the land to seek the lost queen. Hanuman steps forward here, the devoted servant of unmatched wit and might. His courage will soon steal every reader's heart in the tale. Dutt renders the beloved book in plain, faithful English prose throughout. The friendship theme gives the war quest its warm human core.
dutt-ramayana-sundara-kanda:
Sundara Kandam, the beautiful book, belongs wholly to Hanuman in Dutt's 1892 version. The monkey hero leaps the sea to Lanka in one vast bound. His search for the captive Sita drives every page that follows.

Hanuman finds Sita in a grove, gives her Rama's ring, and takes hope back. He lets himself be caught, mocks Ravana, and burns the demon city. His strength, wit, and pure devotion shine at their full height here. Readers have treasured this book above all others in the epic. Dutt's English keeps its speed, fire, and tender core alive.
dutt-ramayana-uttara-kanda:
Uttara Kandam, the last book, closes Dutt's Ramayana in his 1894 version. Rama now rules as king in Ayodhya, loved and just at home. Duty, though, makes the cruelest demand a husband can face.

Rumor forces Rama to send away Sita, the queen he loves deeply. She raises their twin sons in a sage's quiet forest hermitage. The boys sing their father's own epic back to him in court. Triumph curdles into tears as the great tale nears its end. Dutt's full rendering lets English readers feel that parting's full weight at last. The epic ends in sorrow, not simple triumph, here.
dutt-ramayana-yuddha-kanda:
Yuddha Kandam, the book of war, appears in Dutt's 1893 English rendering. Rama's host of monkeys and bears marches south to the sea. A bridge of stones carries them across to Ravana's Lanka.

The great battle for Sita rages in vast, cosmic strokes of war. Heroes fall, giants wake, and Rama faces Ravana at last in duel. Dutt's faithful prose carries the war book's thunder from charge to victory. Right and wrong, not just two armies, clash on Lanka's fields in fire. The scale grows until gods themselves watch the fight below. The rescue of Sita crowns the epic's long arc of exile.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AgendasMemosWar:
On February 6, 1964, the Office of the Director of the FBI sent a memorandum to J. Lee Rankin, general counsel of the Warren Commission. The memo is part of the working traffic between the Bureau and the commission investigating President Kennedy's assassination.

Its job was delivery: it sent affidavits and interview results gathered by FBI agents for the commission's use. The Warren Commission had no staff to speak of and leaned on the Bureau for fieldwork, which made letters like this one its lifeline. The file is kept among the commission's agendas and memos, the paperwork of the inquiry.
govdocs-archive_org-the-poetic-edda:
Medieval Iceland preserved the Poetic Edda, a set of Old Norse poems about gods and heroes, gathered in the thirteenth century. Odin, Thor, Loki, and the Valkyries move through its myth songs, while its heroic lays tell of cursed gold, broken oaths, and doomed lovers.

No single author wrote the Edda. Singers and scribes carried the poems for centuries before they were written down, so each lay keeps an older voice. Nearly everything the modern world knows about Norse mythology starts in these verses. The full text here gives readers the source itself, the world classic behind the retellings, games, and films.
hadda-pada:
Guðmundur Kamban's Hadda Padda is an Icelandic play in English dress, built around one woman's soul. The foreword stakes the whole play on Hadda Padda herself, and declares that she carries it. She holds the play as a saint in old paintings bears the church. In her, ancient and modern Iceland meet.

An old nurse's tale of the life-egg, told over a crystal ball, opens the action. Hadda Padda gives herself completely to a love that the world misjudges. A herb-woman's calm talk of plants recalls Ophelia among her flowers. Kamban weaves superstition, saga pride, and modern feeling into her struggle. She is tender and mild without being meek, the foreword insists. The play made its young author Iceland's modern dramatist, and its heroine a national figure.
in-the-riding-school-chats-with-esmerald:
Theo. Stephenson Browne wrote In the Riding-School as chats with a pupil named Esmeralda, dated 1890. The title page credits the text in the name of G. Hamlin in the catalogue, while chats are signed by Browne. Lessons run from dress and first mounting to trotting and rein holds. Esmeralda's trials at the third lesson get a chapter.

Class rides, music rides, and basic army movements follow. A critic in the gallery watches for bad riding as a double circle sweeps the ring. Elbows high and hands too close earn gentle sarcasm. The book teaches seat and hands through talk.
journal-of-a-voyage-across-the-atlantic-:
George Moore's Journal of a Voyage across the Atlantic records his 1844 trip to Canada and the United States. Moore printed the little volume in London in 1845, for private circulation. He dedicates it to Eliza Moore. In his preface, dated April 30, 1845, he explains that friends urged him to publish his notes.

Moore insists he did not revise or alter impressions formed at the moment. He never saw the notes again, he says, until they passed through the press. The trip, he adds, greatly improved his health. Proud to be an Englishman, he still hopes to do justice to America's wonders. The journal offers a fresh, unpolished English view of North America in the 1840s.
mathilda:
Mary Shelley wrote this short tale of a father's dark love in 1819 and 1820. It did not see print in her life, and was held back by her kin for years. The tale is told in the first person, as a death bed account to a friend.

Mathilda's father owns a love for her that no father should bear for a child. She flees to a lone moor to live with her grief and shame, far from the world. Stark and sad, the tale is the most brave and dark of all Shelley's works.
narada-bhakti-sutras-vivekananda:
The Narada Bhakti Sutras are 84 short sayings on bhakti, the intense love of God, ascribed to the sage Narada. Swami Vivekananda, the Hindu monk who carried Vedanta to the West, dictated this free English version in America. It appeared in print in 1907, after his death.

The sutras define devotion as the highest love, beyond desire for reward and beyond fear. They list its signs, its fruits, and its dangers, and name the company of saints as its surest school. Vivekananda's rendering is loose but fervent, shaped by his own teaching voice. The text is the classic handbook of Hindu devotionalism, small enough to read in one sitting and rich enough to reread for years.
nasa-tm-19660005957-the-interpretation-o:
Lewis J Allison and Guenter Warnecke, at Goddard and on leave from Berlin, show how TIROS radiation data can serve daily weather work. Synoptic analysis is the making of weather maps from many reports at once. TIROS III radiation readings are used here to prove the point in practice. Forecasters were still learning what satellite radiation data could add.

Radiation data reveal where Earth and its clouds give off heat. Read well, they expose storms and clear regions between ground reports. The authors aim at practical use, not theory alone. Their paper helped move satellite data from research desks into the forecaster's daily routine, where it has stayed ever since.
parkman-old-regime-canada:
The Old Régime in Canada, from 1874, portrays French Canada under Louis XIV. Parkman presents Part Four of his great series on two empires. Absolute monarchy crosses the sea and plants itself on the St. Lawrence.

Intendants rule, seigneurs hold land, and priests guide daily life. Parkman shows a society held in feudal forms long past their age. His portrait is brilliant, sharp, and still debated by scholars today. He asks why New France grew so slowly beside the English colonies. The answer he gives shaped how generations read Canadian history and its roots. Few volumes in the series spark more debate than this one.
pioneers-in-canada:
Sir Harry Johnston's Pioneers in Canada, published in 1912 with eight colored illustrations by E. Wallcousins, belongs to his Pioneer Library series on how Europeans opened new lands. This volume traces the white man's coming to North America and the making of Canada.

Chapters follow Jacques Cartier, the Elizabethan pioneers, and Champlain, then move from Montreal toward the Mississippi. Johnston also describes the land itself and its first peoples, the Amerindians and Eskimo, before turning to the Hudson Bay explorers and the British conquest. Later chapters follow Alexander Henry, Samuel Hearne, and Alexander Mackenzie on their journeys. It is a broad, old-style history of exploration, trade, and settlement.
podcast-dannyjones-GHxM8cX_OdA:
Security trainer Ed Calderon joins Danny Jones to warn about cartels and China. Calderon once worked for the Mexican government. He now teaches people to survive in hostile places.

Calderon explains skills for moving through areas gangs control. He argues China uses cartels to weaken the United States. Jones presses him on drugs, precursors, and money flows. The guest ties street crime to a larger state rivalry. The episode blends survival advice with a stark claim about foreign power, drugs, and a border that serves as a front line. His lessons come from hard years on the ground.
podcast-joerogan-_cPD7l1LEDA:
Mystic and teacher Sadhguru sits with Rogan for episode 1791 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Sadhguru founded the Isha Foundation in India and teaches yoga as a science of the inner life. His calm, funny manner has made him a global figure far beyond his ashram.

He and Rogan talk about the mind's habits, the search for joy that does not depend on events, and the discipline of sitting with oneself. Rogan, the restless host, makes a good foil for a guest who answers hurry with stillness. The episode is one of the show's gentlest hours, a talk on the inner life that never raises its voice.
roscoe-baganda:
John Roscoe published The Baganda in 1911 after years in Uganda. His account of native customs and beliefs became a classic at once. The Buganda kingdom stands at the center of his full study.

Kingship, clans, gods, and daily work unfold in rich, ordered detail. Roscoe recorded ways that stood just before deep colonial change. He worked with Baganda helpers who trusted him with their lore. Later scholars treat the book as the model study of its age. It remains the first book to read on old Buganda today for newcomers. Its detail on kingship and clan law still guides research now.
sagard-histoire-canada:
Sagard's Histoire du Canada, in French from 1636, tells the Recollect side of the story. The lay brother recounts his order's voyages and missions in Canada. His book answers, in part, the famed Relations of the Jesuits.

Huron life fills the pages in a voice more raw and personal. Sagard adds humor, hunger, and small mishaps that grand accounts skip. He defends his own order's work while praising the land and people. Readers gain a second, earthier view of early French Canada here. The book ranks among the first great French works on Canada and its peoples. Its voice stays fresh across four centuries of print.
tales-and-novels-volume-03-belinda:
Volume III of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels holds Belinda, her novel of a young woman entering fashionable London life. The printing at hand is dated 1857, and the chapter heads open with Characters and Masks, promising a world of surfaces.

Lady Delacour's history takes the third and fourth chapters, told to Belinda as a warning from inside that glittering world. Birthday dresses, ways and means, a family party, and advice follow, then the mysterious boudoir, difficulties, the macaw, and a fortune-telling game of sortes Virgilianae. Belinda must judge the Delacours' brilliance against plainer worth, choosing what sort of marriage and what sort of character to make her own.
the-principles-of-gothic-ecclesiastical-: The Principles of Gothic Ecclesiastical Architecture, Elucidated by Question and Answer, announces its method in its title. A motto from Dugdale's Antiquities of Warwickshire praises the zeal of elder times, when even the meaner sort endowed the church freely. Transcriber's notes explain that marked typing errors of the original are kept and listed at the end. The leaves provided stop at the title page, so the question-and-answer exposition itself is not shown.
the-prisoner-of-zenda:
Rudolf Rassendyll narrates The Prisoner of Zenda, Anthony Hope's novel, over his sister-in-law's breakfast-table challenge. Rose asks when he will do anything. He answers that his income nearly suffices, his position is enviable, and the Rassendylls do not need to do things. She notes he is nine-and-twenty and has done nothing but knock about. The contents promise the Elphbergs, a king who keeps his appointment, and an understudy's adventures.

Later chapters name the secret of a cellar, a fair cousin and a dark brother, and a new use for a tea-table. The plan grows desperate through a night outside the castle and young Rupert's midnight diversions. The forcing of the trap and a forest meeting lead to the prisoner and the king. The final chapters ask if love were all, and weigh present, past, and future.
the-young-woodsman-or-life-in-the-forest: J. Macdonald Oxley's The Young Woodsman, dated 1895, is shown through its contents and a single opening line. Twelve chapters follow Frank from a call to work into Canada's forests. Building a shanty and life in a lumber camp appear. The great spring drive brings the logs downriver. Chapter one begins with a mother fearing school is over for Frank. The story itself stops at that first line in the pages present.
the-younger-edda-also-called-snorre-s-ed: Rasmus B. Anderson translated The Younger Edda, also called Snorre's Edda or the Prose Edda, in a Chicago edition dated 1901. Title pages explain that the version covers the foreword and The Fooling of Gylfe. Brage's Talk and key passages on poetic diction follow. Anderson adds an introduction, notes, vocabulary, and index. The preface opens with the Norse creation void, Ginungagap. Only the front pages and that opening are present in this record.
troilus-and-cressida:
Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida appears here in old-spelling folio style, titled The Tragedie of Troilus and Cressida. An armed Prologue walks on first. He places the scene at Troy, where sixty-nine crowned Greek princes have sailed against the city over ravished Helen, Menelaus's queen.

The Prologue warns that the play leaps over the first broils and begins in the middle. Act one then opens before Priam's palace, with Troilus calling for his man to unarm him. He asks why he should fight outside Troy's walls when he finds crueller battle within. Love, not war, is his wound, and the play's bitter tone is set at once.
true-tilda: True Tilda, by Q, the pen name of A. T. Quiller-Couch, comes with a transcriber's warning about language. Working-class slang and dialect of a century ago fill the book, with nearly as many apostrophes as letters. Tattoo diagrams in two chapters were replaced by written descriptions. The contents promise a kidnapping, a child actor's embarrassments, and flight and pursuit. Childe Arthur loses one mother and gains another. Only the note and contents are present here, so Tilda's adventures themselves do not appear.
veranilda:
George Gissing set his novel Veranilda in Italy during the Gothic wars. The contents name its people and places. They include Basil, the deacon Leander, Cumae, and the Anicians. Heliodora, a prisoner at Praeneste, and an island in the Liris follow. Rome beleaguered ends the list. Chapter one, The Vanquished Roman, opens the story after seven years of war.

Gissing begins with the war's turn. The armies of the emperor Justinian have fought the Goths across Italy. The great commander Belisarius, victor from Rhegium to Ravenna, has gone back to the East. He carried a captured Gothic king with him. Rome stands between two worlds, pagan and Christian, Roman and Goth. Basil, a young Roman, and Veranilda, a Gothic maiden, give the history its human thread. Readers get careful period detail in service of a love story under siege.
wakulla-a-story-of-adventure-in-florida:
Kirk Munroe wrote Wakulla, a story of adventure in Florida for young readers. Its contents promise a schooner called Nancy Bell and a wreck on the Florida reef. A queer Christmas day, a ghost found in a trying position, and a runaway's happy ending follow. A mill picnic, a forest fire, and the capture of an alligator come later. One chapter buries a boy in an underground river. Chapter one opens in the north, where Mark and Ruth Elmer read one newspaper item again and again.

The item reports that their father, Mark Elmer, is in delicate health and must move to a warmer climate. He has sold his property and bought a plantation in Florida. The family will settle there at once. The children thus trade a northern home for wild Florida, among rivers, reefs, and pine woods. Each chapter brings a fresh scrape.
woman-triumphant-la-maja-desnuda: Vicente Blasco Ibanez wrote this Spanish novel, rendered into English by Hayward Keniston. Pages present here hold title pages and a list of nine printings, all dated March and April 1920. The title page promises a special introductory note by the author. That note and all story text stay absent from these pages. The English title pairs triumph with the Spanish title La Maja Desnuda, naming a famed painted figure.
